missions/asteroid/hayabusa2.json.name: Hayabusa2
missions/asteroid/hayabusa2.json.payload: 609 kg dry, ion-electric propulsion (4×μ10 thrusters) + chemical bipropellant + 1.6 m HGA. Onboard payload — Small Carry-on Impactor (SCI, 2.5 kg shaped charge), MASCOT lander (10 kg, DLR/CNES), 3× MINERVA-II rovers (~1 kg each), sample return capsule (16 kg, parachute reentry).
missions/asteroid/hayabusa2.json.first: Second asteroid sample return (Ryugu, 2020); first artificial impact crater on an asteroid; first subsurface asteroid material returned to Earth
missions/asteroid/hayabusa2.json.description: JAXA's follow-on to the original Hayabusa. Launched 2014-12-03, Hayabusa2 reached carbonaceous near-Earth asteroid (162173) Ryugu on 2018-06-27 after a 3.5-year low-thrust ion cruise + Earth gravity assist. Surface operations 2018–2019: two touchdown-and-go sample collections bracketing a Small Carry-on Impactor experiment (2019-04-05) that excavated a 14 m crater for the second sample. Three MINERVA-II rovers returned the first surface images from an asteroid; the DLR/CNES MASCOT lander operated for 17 hours. Sample return capsule reentry over Woomera on 2020-12-05 (UTC; recovered 2020-12-06 local/JST) delivered 5.4 g of pristine Ryugu material — the first asteroid sample with subsurface stratigraphy. Extended mission: flyby of 98943 Torifune (2001 CC21) in 2026-07; rendezvous with fast-rotating (1998 KY26) targeted for 2031-07.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: H-IIA 202 from Tanegashima begins the 3.5-year cruise to asteroid Ryugu.

events.label: EARTH FLYBY
events.note: Earth gravity assist phases the rendezvous orbit.

events.label: RYUGU ARRIVAL
events.note: Hover at 20 km — start of 1.5-year proximity operations including sample collection.

events.label: EARTH RETURN
events.note: Sample capsule lands in Woomera, Australia with 5.4 g of Ryugu material.

events.label: TORIFUNE FLYBY
events.note: Extended-mission flyby of 98943 Torifune (2001 CC21).

events.label: 1998 KY26 RENDEZVOUS
events.note: Planned rendezvous with fast-rotating asteroid (1998 KY26).

missions/asteroid/near-shoemaker.json.name: NEAR Shoemaker
missions/asteroid/near-shoemaker.json.payload: 805 kg at launch (487 kg dry) — X-ray/gamma-ray spectrometer, near-infrared spectrograph, multispectral camera, laser rangefinder (LIDAR), magnetometer. First spacecraft to orbit and land on an asteroid.
missions/asteroid/near-shoemaker.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit an asteroid (433 Eros, 2000) and first soft landing on any small body (2001-02-12)
missions/asteroid/near-shoemaker.json.dispatch: NEAR Shoemaker went to Eros because nobody knew what an asteroid really looked like up close. It arrived to find a world pocked with craters, stretched into a saddle shape by its own slow rotation, covered in fine regolith that had nowhere to go in near-zero gravity. For a year it mapped every ridge and boulder from orbit, then in February 2001 the controllers pressed their luck: they lowered the spacecraft's orbit five times in two weeks, slowed it to walking pace, and set it down on the surface. It survived. For sixteen more days it transmitted from Eros — the first emissary from Earth to rest on a small body.
missions/asteroid/near-shoemaker.json.description: NASA Discovery-program mission, led by Johns Hopkins University APL. Launched 1996-02-17, NEAR Shoemaker flew past asteroid 253 Mathilde (1997-06-27) before an Earth gravity assist (1998-01-23) phased its orbit to match Eros. Orbital insertion around 433 Eros on 2000-02-14 began a 12-month survey that returned 160,000 images and complete spectral, compositional, and gravitational maps of the 34 × 11 × 11 km S-type body. On 2001-02-12, five orbit-lowering burns brought the spacecraft to 5 km altitude; controlled descent at ~1.7 m/s ended with a soft landing near the Himeros saddle (35°N, 280°W), returning images to within 125 m of the surface. The spacecraft survived and transmitted from the surface for ~16 days.

events.label: LAUNCH — DELTA II
events.note: Cape Canaveral, 1996-02-17. First Discovery-program planetary mission.

events.label: 253 MATHILDE FLYBY
events.note: 1997-06-27: 1,212 km flyby of carbonaceous asteroid Mathilde; 500 images.

events.label: EARTH GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: 1998-01-23: 540 km flyby phases the orbit to match Eros.

events.label: EROS ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: 2000-02-14: first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid; 12 months of orbital science.

events.label: EROS LANDING — EDL
events.note: 2001-02-12: controlled descent at 1.7 m/s — first soft landing on any small body.

missions/bennu/osiris-rex.json.name: OSIRIS-REx
missions/bennu/osiris-rex.json.first: Largest asteroid sample ever returned (121.6 g of Bennu, delivered to Earth 2023-09-24)
missions/bennu/osiris-rex.json.description: OSIRIS-REx carried out one of the most exacting asteroid-proximity operations ever attempted. Launched 2016-09-08 from Cape Canaveral on an Atlas V 411, used a 2017 Earth gravity assist to rotate its orbital plane onto Bennu's 6° inclination, and rendezvoused with the 492-m carbonaceous near-Earth asteroid 2018-12-03. After stationkeeping at ~19 km, it later entered a record ~1.4 km orbit — the closest spacecraft orbit ever around any celestial body. Spent two years mapping Bennu's boulder-strewn surface and discovering active particle ejections. 2020-10-20 the Touch-and-Go sample arm descended to the Nightingale site, fired N₂ gas into the surface, and grabbed a plume — sinking 50 cm into a 'rubble-pile fluid' surface. Sample Return Capsule delivered 121.6 g of Bennu material to Utah 2023-09-24. The spacecraft itself was immediately redesignated OSIRIS-APEX, en route to a 2029 Apophis rendezvous.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 411 from Cape Canaveral SLC-41.

events.label: EARTH GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: 2017-09-22, 17,237 km over Antarctica — rotates orbital plane onto Bennu's 6° inclination.

events.label: BENNU RENDEZVOUS
events.note: Arrives at Bennu; stationkeeps at ~19 km then progressively tightens to a record ~1.4 km orbit — closest spacecraft orbit ever around any celestial body.

events.label: TAG SAMPLE COLLECTION
events.note: 2020-10-20. Touch-and-Go arm sinks 50 cm into the rubble-pile surface; grabs 121.6 g.

events.label: BENNU DEPARTURE
events.note: 2021-05-10. 2.5-year cruise back to Earth.

events.label: SAMPLE RETURN
events.note: 2023-09-24. SRC parachutes into Utah Test and Training Range; spacecraft becomes OSIRIS-APEX.

missions/ceres/dawn.json.name: Dawn
missions/ceres/dawn.json.payload: Ion-propelled orbiter; framing camera, VIR, GRaND, etc.
missions/ceres/dawn.json.first: First mission to orbit two extraterrestrial bodies — Vesta, then Ceres
missions/ceres/dawn.json.description: Dawn proved ion propulsion at planetary scale: it matched orbits with massive Vesta, left, and spiralled down onto dwarf planet Ceres — the largest object in the asteroid belt. Bright spots in Occator crater became one of the mission's iconic mysteries, later tied to briny eruptions from a deep reservoir. This catalogue entry uses Ceres as the primary destination; Vesta is covered in the narrative above.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Delta II lifts Dawn toward Vesta and Ceres on a low-thrust spiral highway.

events.label: CERES CAPTURE
events.note: Ion engines brake Dawn into orbit around Ceres; mapping campaign begins.

missions/comet/giotto.json.name: Giotto
missions/comet/giotto.json.payload: 960 kg spin-stabilised drum-shaped probe with a layered Whipple-Kevlar dust shield (rear bumper kept the science instruments live through the 68 km/s relative-velocity dust storm of the Halley coma). 10 instruments — Halley Multicolour Camera, mass spectrometers, dust impact detectors, magnetometer, plasma instruments.
missions/comet/giotto.json.first: ESA's first deep-space mission; closest comet flyby ever attempted (Halley, 596 km, 1986); first close-up imaging of a cometary nucleus
missions/comet/giotto.json.description: Giotto was Europe's pillar of the Halley armada — a spin-stabilised 960 kg probe wrapped in a layered Whipple-Kevlar dust shield. Launched 1985-07-02, it flew through Halley's coma at 68 km/s relative velocity on 1986-03-14 with closest approach 596 km, returning the first close-up images of any cometary nucleus (an irregular 15 × 7.2 × 7.2 km elongated body with concentrated dust jets). A dust impact ~7.6 seconds before closest approach destabilised the spin axis and killed the camera, but the other instruments kept transmitting through the coma. After hibernating in heliocentric orbit, Giotto reactivated 1990 + used Earth gravity assist to retarget to comet 26P/Grigg-Skjellerup, flying past it at 200 km on 1992-07-10 — the closest cometary flyby ever performed.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Ariane 1 lifts Giotto from Kourou — ESA's first deep-space mission.

events.label: HALLEY FLYBY
events.note: 596 km closest approach to comet 1P/Halley; first close-up imagery of a cometary nucleus.

events.label: EARTH FLYBY
events.note: Earth gravity assist retargets Giotto to comet 26P/Grigg-Skjellerup.

events.label: GRIGG-SKJELLERUP FLYBY
events.note: 200 km closest approach — the closest cometary flyby on record.

missions/comet/rosetta.json.name: Rosetta
missions/comet/rosetta.json.payload: Orbiter (~2900 kg dry, 11 instruments) + Philae descent lander (~100 kg, 10 instruments). Heatshield, two Earth + one Mars gravity assist, 957 days of deep-space hibernation 2011–2014.
missions/comet/rosetta.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit a comet — and to land on one (Philae, 2014-11-12)
missions/comet/rosetta.json.description: ESA's flagship comet-rendezvous mission. After a 10-year cruise that wove three Earth assists, a Mars assist, two asteroid flybys, and 957 days of deep-space hibernation, Rosetta caught up with comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko in August 2014 and orbited it for over two years through perihelion and out the back side. The Philae lander reached 67P's surface 2014-11-12 — the first soft landing on a comet — and returned ~64 hours of science after a harpoon failure left it in the shadow of a cliff. Rosetta itself ended the mission with a controlled descent to 67P's surface on 2016-09-30. Key results: organic molecules and glycine in the coma; 67P's initially-measured D/H ratio (≈3× terrestrial) argued against Jupiter-family comets as Earth's water source — a result a 2024 re-analysis has since called into question after finding a measurement error; the first detailed maps of comet outgassing geometry.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Ariane 5G+ lifts Rosetta from Kourou for the 10-year cruise to comet 67P.

events.label: EARTH FLYBY #1
events.note: First of three Earth gravity assists to build velocity for the comet rendezvous.

events.label: MARS FLYBY
events.note: Single Mars gravity assist + first close imagery of Phobos and Mars at 250 km.

events.label: ASTEROID 2867 ŠTEINS
events.note: First-ever close-up of an E-type asteroid.

events.label: ASTEROID 21 LUTETIA
events.note: ~120 km flyby of one of the largest main-belt asteroids ever observed close-up.

events.label: COMET 67P RENDEZVOUS
events.note: Orbit insertion around comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. Philae lands 2014-11-12.

missions/didymos/hera.json.name: Hera
missions/didymos/hera.json.first: ESA's follow-up to DART — surveying the deflected Didymos asteroid
missions/didymos/hera.json.description: Hera is the European Space Agency's contribution to humanity's first planetary-defence experiment. In 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos — the small moon of the asteroid Didymos — and measurably shortened its orbit. Hera, launched in October 2024 on a Falcon 9, is flying to the same binary asteroid (with a 2025 Mars gravity assist en route) to conduct the detailed post-impact survey DART couldn't: the size of the crater, Dimorphos's mass and internal structure, and precisely how much momentum the impact transferred. Together, DART and Hera turn a one-off demonstration into a repeatable, well-characterised deflection technique. Hera carries two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, for close-up radar sounding and mineralogy.

missions/dimorphos/dart.json.name: DART
missions/dimorphos/dart.json.payload: 611 kg (incl. ~60 kg xenon for NEXT-C ion thruster demonstrator + ~50 kg hydrazine)
missions/dimorphos/dart.json.first: First demonstration of kinetic-impactor planetary defense; first time humans moved an asteroid
missions/dimorphos/dart.json.description: DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) was the first planetary-defense mission ever flown — a 611-kg spacecraft sent to hit a 160-m asteroid hard enough to change its orbit. The target was Dimorphos, a moonlet of the 780-m asteroid Didymos. Launched 2021-11-24 on a Falcon 9; the SMART Nav autonomous navigation system took over 4 hours before impact to distinguish Dimorphos from its parent and target the smaller body. Impact 2022-09-26 at 23:14 UTC at ~6.6 km/s. Measured orbital-period change: 33 minutes (4.2%), exceeding the 73-second success threshold by ~25×. Momentum-transfer enhancement factor β ≈ 3.6 indicated significant carry from ejected surface material. The CubeSat LICIACube observed the plume; HST and JWST imaged the resulting ejecta tail for weeks. First demonstration that humans can move an asteroid.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Falcon 9 Block 5 from Vandenberg SLC-4E.

events.label: MID-CRUISE
events.note: TCM + NEXT-C ion-thruster demonstration firings.

events.label: APPROACH
events.note: 2022-09-26. SMART Nav takes over 4h pre-impact.

events.label: IMPACT
events.note: 23:14 UTC. ~6.6 km/s. 33-min orbital-period change — first deflection of an asteroid by humans.

events.label: LOSS OF SIGNAL
events.note: LICIACube + HST + JWST observe the ejecta plume.

missions/earth/apollo-1.json.name: Apollo 1 (AS-204)
missions/earth/apollo-1.json.payload: Apollo CSM-012 (Block I) — burned on pad
missions/earth/apollo-1.json.first: Fatal pre-launch pad fire 1967-01-27 killed Grissom + White + Chaffee
missions/earth/apollo-1.json.description: Apollo 1 was the planned first crewed flight of the Apollo Block I CSM, originally designated AS-204 and scheduled to launch 1967-02-21 from LC-34. During a routine "plugs-out" test on 1967-01-27 17:31 EST, with the crew sealed inside the pressurised pure-oxygen cabin, a flash fire ignited in the lower-equipment bay — likely a Teflon-insulated wire arc through silver-plated copper that had been damaged during installation. Cabin pressure spiked to 29 psi within 15 seconds; the inward-opening hatch couldn't be unsealed against the pressure differential. Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died from asphyxiation within seconds. The investigation led to a complete Block I → Block II redesign + the safer outward-opening unified hatch + non-flammable cabin materials + pre-launch nitrogen-rich cabin atmosphere. Apollo 1's official designation was assigned posthumously to honour the crew. Subsequent Apollo missions (CSM-101 through CSM-114) flew the Block II hardware that this redesign produced.

events.label: PAD FIRE
events.note: Plugs-out test 1967-01-27 17:31 EST. Flash fire in pressurised pure-O₂ cabin; cabin pressure spiked to 29 psi in 15 s.

events.label: CREW LOST
events.note: Grissom + White + Chaffee perish from asphyxiation. Hatch could not be unsealed against pressure differential.

events.label: PROGRAM PAUSE
events.note: Apollo crewed program halted 21 months. Mission renamed Apollo 1 in posthumous honour.

missions/earth/apollo-soyuz.json.name: Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP)
missions/earth/apollo-soyuz.json.payload: Apollo CSM-111 (last Apollo CSM ever) + Soyuz 19 (modified 7K-TM); 14.4 t Apollo + 6.8 t Soyuz
missions/earth/apollo-soyuz.json.first: First international human spaceflight cooperation; first US-USSR rendezvous + docking
missions/earth/apollo-soyuz.json.dispatch: Apollo-Soyuz is where the space race ends — not at a finish line, but with a handshake. In July 1975 an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz, the rival spacecraft of the rival superpowers, met and docked in orbit, and Tom Stafford and Alexei Leonov shook hands through the open hatch between them. It took a jointly-built docking adapter, two crews learning each other's language, and a thaw in the Cold War deep enough to let the era's fiercest competitors cooperate in full view of the world. Nothing about it was strictly necessary; that was the point. After eighteen years of racing to be first, the two programs chose, for one flight, simply to meet — and set the template for the international cooperation that would one day build the Space Station.
missions/earth/apollo-soyuz.json.description: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project — first international crewed spaceflight, first US-USSR rendezvous + docking, and the final flight of an Apollo CSM. Apollo (Stafford + Brand + Slayton) launched 1975-07-15 from LC-39B; Soyuz 19 (Leonov + Kubasov) launched the same day from Baikonur. Apollo's docking module (built by NASA + Rockwell) used a new androgynous docking ring (APAS) that allowed either spacecraft to be active — the precursor of every international docking system since (Mir, ISS, Tiangong, Dragon, Starliner). Hatch opening 1975-07-17 ~16:00 UTC; the crews exchanged flags, gifts, and joint experiments across 2 dockings (initial July 17, practice July 19) totalling ~44 hours docked. Soyuz returned 1975-07-21; Apollo continued 5 more days in orbit before splashdown 1975-07-24 — last Apollo splashdown ever. CSM-111 is on display at the California Science Center, LA (alongside Endeavour). The détente-era cooperation that ASTP modelled informed the Shuttle-Mir programme 20 years later.

events.label: LAUNCH (Apollo)
events.note: Saturn IB (AS-210) from LC-39B 1975-07-15 19:50 UTC. 7.5 h after Soyuz 19 (Baikonur 1975-07-15 12:20 UTC).

events.label: DOCKING
events.note: Apollo + Soyuz 19 dock 1975-07-17 16:09 UTC. First US-USSR rendezvous + dock. Hatch opens 19:17 UTC; Stafford–Leonov handshake ~3 hours later (~22:19 UTC).

events.label: JOINT OPS
events.note: Flag + gift exchange; joint experiments; 2 dockings across ~44 hours docked.

events.label: UNDOCK
events.note: Final undock 1975-07-19 16:26 UTC. Soyuz 19 lands 1975-07-21 in Kazakhstan.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN (Apollo)
events.note: Apollo splashed down in Pacific 1975-07-24 21:18 UTC — last Apollo splashdown ever, and the last US crewed water landing until SpaceX Crew Dragon in 2020. CSM-111 displayed at California Science Center LA.

missions/earth/apollo7.json.name: Apollo 7
missions/earth/apollo7.json.first: First crewed Apollo flight — Earth-orbit CSM shakedown
missions/earth/apollo7.json.description: The first crewed Apollo flight, 21 months after the Apollo 1 fire (1967-01-27) killed Grissom, White and Chaffee on the pad. Apollo 7 verified the redesigned Block II Command and Service Module in Earth orbit — life support, power, propulsion (SPS fired eight times), thermal control, and the world's first live TV broadcast from a crewed US spacecraft. Schirra (head cold + irritable throughout) overruled Houston on a re-entry helmet question, contributing to Mission Control's decision that none of the three crewmembers would fly again. The 10 day 20 hour flight cleared the way for Apollo 8's lunar-orbit gamble two months later.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Saturn IB (AS-205) from Cape Kennedy LC-34 1968-10-11 15:02 UTC.

events.label: ORBIT INSERT
events.note: CSM separates from S-IVB into 232 × 285 km Earth orbit, inclination 31.6°. SPS firing sequence (8 burns over 11 days) validates the propulsion that will perform LOI + TEI at the Moon.

events.label: FIRST LIVE TV
events.note: "Hello from the lovely Apollo room high atop everything." First live TV broadcast from a crewed US spacecraft.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: CM splashed down in the North Atlantic 1968-10-22 11:11 UTC after 163 orbits / 7.4 million km / 10 d 20 h. Recovery by USS Essex.

missions/earth/apollo9.json.name: Apollo 9
missions/earth/apollo9.json.first: First crewed LM flight — Earth-orbit LM separation + rendezvous tests
missions/earth/apollo9.json.description: The first crewed flight of the Lunar Module. In Earth orbit, McDivitt and Schweickart undocked LM Spider from CSM Gumdrop, flew up to 183 km away over six hours, then rendezvous and re-docked — every step of the lunar-rendezvous procedure tested without the option of bringing the crew home in the CSM if anything went wrong. Schweickart did a 38-minute EVA on the LM porch, demonstrating the Apollo EVA spacesuit + PLSS backpack design that the Moonwalking crews would use. Scott did a stand-up EVA from the CSM hatch. With LM hardware and rendezvous procedures verified, NASA was clear to send Apollo 10 to the Moon two months later.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Saturn V (AS-504) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39A 1969-03-03 16:00 UTC — third Saturn V flight, first crewed launch carrying LM.

events.label: CSM-LM EXTRACTION
events.note: CSM Gumdrop turns around + docks with LM Spider in the SLA adapter — first crewed transposition + docking. All Apollo lunar missions repeat this maneuver.

events.label: LM SEPARATION
events.note: McDivitt + Schweickart undock Spider, fly up to 183 km from Gumdrop over six hours. First crewed flight where the spacecraft + crew aren't both attached to a re-entry vehicle.

events.label: EVA
events.note: Schweickart does 38-min EVA on LM porch. Scott stand-up EVA from CSM hatch. First validation of Apollo PLSS backpack.

events.label: RENDEZVOUS + REDOCK
events.note: Spider rendezvous + redocks with Gumdrop, completing the lunar-procedure dress rehearsal in Earth orbit.

events.label: LM JETTISON
events.note: Spider descent stage deorbited (reentered March 1969, Indian Ocean); ascent stage was fired to depletion and boosted to a high orbit — it decayed 1981.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: CM splashed down in North Atlantic 1969-03-13 17:00 UTC after 151 orbits. Recovery by USS Guadalcanal.

missions/earth/artemis3.json.name: Artemis III
missions/earth/artemis3.json.vehicle: SLS Block 1 (with a non-propulsive spacer in place of the upper stage)
missions/earth/artemis3.json.payload: Orion + 4-person crew; rendezvous and docking with pathfinder Starship and Blue Moon landers in low Earth orbit
missions/earth/artemis3.json.first: First crewed test of the commercial lunar landers — Orion docks with them in Earth orbit
missions/earth/artemis3.json.description: Artemis III no longer lands on the Moon. In February 2026 NASA changed the plan: before risking a landing, a crew will fly Orion in low Earth orbit and rehearse the hardest new step — rendezvous and docking with the commercial landers that will later carry astronauts to the surface. SLS launches Orion with four crew, flying with a spacer in place of its upper stage, since no push towards the Moon is needed. In orbit, Orion meets pathfinder versions of SpaceX's Starship lander and Blue Origin's Blue Moon, docks, and the crew test the joined vehicles' life support, communications and propulsion, along with the new AxEMU spacesuits. The flight lasts about two weeks. It plays the part Apollo 9 played in 1969, when the lunar module was flown and docked in Earth orbit before anyone took it to the Moon. Crew, named in June 2026: Randy Bresnik (commander), Luca Parmitano of ESA (pilot), Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio. NASA plans the flight for 2027.

missions/earth/aurora-7.json.name: Aurora 7 / MA-7
missions/earth/aurora-7.json.first: Repeated Glenn's 3-orbit profile; overshot landing target by 400 km
missions/earth/aurora-7.json.dispatch: Aurora 7 was meant to be a repeat and became a scare. Scott Carpenter flew the same three-orbit profile as Glenn, but distracted by experiments and a balky control system he burned through his attitude fuel and fired his retros a few seconds late and slightly out of line — enough to carry him some 400 kilometres past his landing target. For a long, silent hour no one knew whether he was alive, until a search plane spotted him bobbing in a life raft. It is a plain reminder that in a machine with almost no margin, small errors compound fast — and that recovering from them is a skill of its own.
missions/earth/aurora-7.json.description: Scott Carpenter's 3-orbit flight — repeated Glenn's MA-6 profile to firm up confidence in the Mercury-Atlas vehicle before attempting the longer Schirra/Cooper flights. Carpenter ran extensive zero-g experiments and observation tasks; the heavy experimental load + a stuck yaw thruster caused him to be ~25° off attitude at retro-fire, overshooting the landing target by ~400 km. The 1 h 7 min recovery delay was widely reported and damaged Carpenter's reputation in NASA management; he never flew again. Capsule Aurora 7 on display at the Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago IL.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas LV-3B from Cape Canaveral LC-14 1962-05-24 12:45 UTC.

events.label: ORBIT INSERT
events.note: Insertion into 161 × 268 km Earth orbit.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: Atlantic Ocean ~400 km past target; 1 h 7 min recovery delay. USS Pierce, USS Intrepid.

missions/earth/faith-7.json.name: Faith 7 / MA-9
missions/earth/faith-7.json.payload: Mercury capsule #20 (1376 kg dry); Gordon Cooper
missions/earth/faith-7.json.first: Last solo American crewed spaceflight; 22 orbits / 34 hours
missions/earth/faith-7.json.dispatch: Faith 7 closed Mercury, and did it the hard way. Gordon Cooper flew twenty-two orbits over a day and a half — longer than every previous Mercury flight combined — and then, in the final hours, his automatic control system failed. So he flew the reentry by hand, lining the capsule up against the horizon and the stars and firing his retros on a spoken count, and put it down closer to the ship than any flight before. It was the last time an American flew in space alone, and a fitting last word for a program built by test pilots: when the automation quit, the pilot brought it home.
missions/earth/faith-7.json.description: Gordon Cooper's 22-orbit flight — last Mercury mission and last solo American spaceflight ever (all subsequent US programmes flew multi-person crews). Duration 34 h 19 min — more than all previous Mercury flights combined. Cooper conducted Earth observation, photography, and ate the first meal in space. Late in the mission a power-supply failure forced manual control of all attitude + retro-fire — Cooper used the window's painted alignment marks against Earth's horizon for orientation, achieving the most accurate splashdown of any Mercury flight (~7 km from target). Capsule Faith 7 on display at Space Center Houston, TX.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas LV-3B from Cape Canaveral LC-14 1963-05-15 13:04 UTC.

events.label: ORBIT INSERT
events.note: Insertion into 161 × 267 km Earth orbit.

events.label: POWER FAILURE
events.note: Power-supply failure; Cooper switches to manual attitude control + retro-fire — earned his "best stick" reputation.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: Pacific Ocean ~7 km from target after 22 orbits / 34 h 19 min. Recovery by USS Kearsarge.

missions/earth/freedom-7.json.name: Freedom 7 / MR-3
missions/earth/freedom-7.json.dispatch: Freedom 7 is where American human spaceflight begins. Three weeks after Gagarin had already orbited the Earth, Alan Shepard's flight was shorter, lower, and slower — fifteen minutes, straight up and straight back down, never even reaching orbit — and the country celebrated anyway, because for the first time an American had left the planet. What set it apart from Gagarin's flight was the man: Shepard hand-flew his capsule's attitude in space, where Gagarin had ridden a fully automated one, and to a program built around test pilots that difference was everything. Twenty days later, its success gave Kennedy the nerve to stand before Congress and bet the nation on the Moon. A small flight that started something very large.
missions/earth/freedom-7.json.description: Alan Shepard's 15-minute suborbital flight — first American in space, 23 days after Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 orbital flight. Apogee 187 km; max-g 11.6 g during re-entry; max-Q 3.7 g. Capsule Freedom 7 splashed down 487 km downrange in the Atlantic. Shepard reportedly remarked "What a beautiful view" at apogee. The flight was suborbital because the Mercury-Redstone launcher couldn't reach orbital velocity; subsequent orbital Mercury missions used the more powerful Atlas LV-3B. Capsule Freedom 7 is on display at the JFK Presidential Library, Boston MA.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Mercury-Redstone 3 (MR-3) from Cape Canaveral LC-5 1961-05-05 14:34 UTC.

events.label: APOGEE
events.note: Apogee 187 km after 2.5 minutes; weightlessness for ~5 min.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: Capsule splashed down 487 km downrange in Atlantic Ocean. Recovery by USS Lake Champlain.

missions/earth/friendship-7.json.name: Friendship 7 / MA-6
missions/earth/friendship-7.json.first: First American to orbit the Earth
missions/earth/friendship-7.json.dispatch: Friendship 7 is the flight where the United States finally caught its breath. John Glenn was the first American to orbit — three times around the planet, ten months after Gagarin — and for a country that had spent four years watching the Soviets go first, that was enough to make him the most famous man in the nation overnight. The drama came near the end: a faulty sensor suggested his heat shield might be loose, and controllers had him keep his spent retro-pack strapped on through reentry as a long shot to hold it in place. It held. Glenn came home, and the anxiety that had hung over the whole program lifted with him.
missions/earth/friendship-7.json.description: John Glenn's 3-orbit flight — first American to orbit Earth, 10 months after Gagarin and 4 months after Titov. Orbit: 159 × 265 km, inclination 32.5°. A heat-shield warning indicator in mission control suggested the shield might be loose — the retropack was kept attached through re-entry as a backup, prompting Glenn's famous "fireflies" observation as bits of retropack ablated past the window. Splashdown 1287 km southeast of Cape Canaveral, 4 h 55 min after launch. Glenn returned to space 36 years later on STS-95 (1998) at age 77. Friendship 7 on display at the National Air and Space Museum, Washington DC.

missions/earth/gemini12.json.name: Gemini 12 / GT-12
missions/earth/gemini12.json.first: Solved EVA — Aldrin's spacewalks; final Gemini
missions/earth/gemini12.json.dispatch: By the last Gemini, one problem was still unsolved: spacewalking didn't work. The flights between Ed White and Gemini 12 had turned EVA into a series of exhausting near-failures — astronauts fighting for every motion, overheating, running out of time. Buzz Aldrin fixed it, and the fix was preparation: he rehearsed the whole thing underwater until it was routine, and the spacecraft was fitted with handholds, footholds, and tethers so he had something to work against. Across more than five hours outside, he did ordinary tasks calmly and came back unspent — proof that EVA could be made reliable. It was the final item on the Gemini checklist, and with it the program closed, having taught NASA everything the Moon would require.
missions/earth/gemini12.json.description: James Lovell and Buzz Aldrin flew the final Gemini, 11-15 November 1966. Aldrin's three EVAs totalling 5 h 30 m — supported by underwater training, handholds, and foot restraints — finally showed that useful work could be done in space, solving the EVA difficulties of earlier flights. 59 orbits.

events.note: Titan II GLV (GT-12) from Cape Canaveral LC-19, 1966-11-11 20:46 UTC.

events.label: EVA MASTERED
events.note: Aldrin's EVAs (5 h 30 m total) with handholds + underwater training prove spacewalking can be routine.

missions/earth/gemini3.json.name: Gemini 3 / GT-3
missions/earth/gemini3.json.payload: Gemini 3 'Molly Brown'; Gus Grissom & John Young
missions/earth/gemini3.json.first: First crewed Gemini; first orbital maneuver by a crew
missions/earth/gemini3.json.dispatch: Gemini 3 was the shakedown — the first flight of the new two-seat spacecraft, and the first time an American crew changed their own orbit rather than just riding the one the rocket gave them. Gus Grissom commanded it, four years after his Mercury capsule sank on splashdown, and named this one "Molly Brown" after the unsinkable heroine — a piece of gallows humor NASA's public-affairs office did not love. The flight itself was short and deliberately modest, three orbits to prove the machine flew as designed. But that small act of nudging the orbit with onboard thrusters was the first step of everything Gemini existed to do.
missions/earth/gemini3.json.description: First crewed Gemini flight. Gus Grissom and John Young flew three orbits on 23 March 1965, checking out the new two-person spacecraft and performing the first orbital maneuver by a crewed vehicle — firing thrusters to change the orbit. Grissom nicknamed the capsule "Molly Brown." Duration 4 h 52 m; Atlantic splashdown.

events.label: ORBIT MANEUVER
events.note: First orbital maneuver by a crew — thrusters change the orbit shape.

missions/earth/gemini4.json.name: Gemini 4 / GT-4
missions/earth/gemini4.json.dispatch: Gemini 4 is remembered for one photograph: Ed White, tethered to the spacecraft by a gold umbilical, floating over a blue Earth with a handheld maneuvering gun — the first American to walk in space. The moment was so exhilarating that when Mission Control ordered him back inside after twenty minutes, White called it the saddest moment of his life. The spacewalk looked effortless and mostly was, because White was drifting free rather than working — the hard truth that EVA is exhausting labor wouldn't arrive until the next few flights. But for a country that had been trailing the Soviets, who had made the first spacewalk eleven weeks earlier, it was proof America could do this too, and the image became one of the defining pictures of the era.
missions/earth/gemini4.json.description: James McDivitt and Edward White flew a four-day, 62-orbit mission from 3 June 1965. During the third orbit White made the first American spacewalk — about 23 minutes outside, tethered, using a handheld maneuvering unit. The flight also ran the first US extended medical + science program.

missions/earth/gemini6a.json.name: Gemini 6A / GT-6A
missions/earth/gemini6a.json.dispatch: Rendezvous — two spacecraft finding and joining each other in orbit — was the skill Apollo could not do without, and Gemini 6A is where it was first done. It nearly didn't fly: its original target blew up on the way to orbit, and then, strapped in for the rescheduled launch, the Titan's engines lit and abruptly died on the pad — a moment when the rules said eject, and Wally Schirra, feeling no motion, coolly chose not to. Three days later it flew and did the thing that had never been done: caught up with Gemini 7 and held station a foot away, the crews close enough to read each other's faces. It looked easy and was anything but — the orbital mechanics of catching another craft are deeply counter-intuitive — and cracking it was the moment lunar-orbit rendezvous, and the whole Apollo plan, became real.
missions/earth/gemini6a.json.description: Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford achieved the first crewed space rendezvous on 15 December 1965, station-keeping within ~30 cm of Gemini 7 for over five hours. It followed a launch-pad engine shutdown three days earlier that Schirra chose not to abort. Duration ~1 d 1 h; 16 orbits.

events.label: RENDEZVOUS

events.label: SPLASHDOWN

missions/earth/gemini7.json.name: Gemini 7 / GT-7
missions/earth/gemini7.json.first: 14-day endurance flight; rendezvous target for Gemini 6A
missions/earth/gemini7.json.dispatch: Gemini 7 answered the least glamorous but most fundamental question: could a crew survive as long as a trip to the Moon and back? Frank Borman and Jim Lovell spent fourteen days sealed in a cabin the size of the front seat of a small car — no room to stand, stretch, or escape each other — to prove the human body and mind could take it. It was tedious and physically miserable, and it worked: they came back healthy, retiring the fear that long spaceflight might be impossible. Along the way they doubled as the target for Gemini 6A's rendezvous, so the single flight quietly proved two of Apollo's prerequisites at once — that people could last the distance, and that two ships could meet.
missions/earth/gemini7.json.description: Frank Borman and Jim Lovell flew a 14-day, 206-orbit endurance mission from 4 December 1965 — the longest crewed spaceflight to that date — and served as the rendezvous target for Gemini 6A. It demonstrated that a crew could withstand spaceflight of full lunar-mission duration.

events.label: RENDEZVOUS TARGET

events.note: Atlantic splashdown after 14 days / 206 orbits.

missions/earth/gemini8.json.name: Gemini 8 / GT-8
missions/earth/gemini8.json.first: First docking of two spacecraft; emergency return
missions/earth/gemini8.json.dispatch: Gemini 8 made the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit — and then nearly killed its crew. Minutes after Neil Armstrong eased his Gemini into a locked joint with an Agena target, the linked pair began to roll, faster and faster, until it was tumbling roughly once a second and the astronauts' vision was starting to gray toward blackout. Armstrong undocked — which only made it worse, since the fault was in his own spacecraft — then shut down the main thrusters and stopped the spin with the reentry-control system, a decision that saved their lives but, by the rules, forced an immediate emergency return. It was the program's most dangerous moment, and it was Armstrong's first spaceflight. The calm, fast diagnosis under a failing situation is exactly the temperament NASA would remember when it chose who would land on the Moon.
missions/earth/gemini8.json.description: Neil Armstrong and David Scott achieved the first docking of two spacecraft — with an Agena target — on 16 March 1966. A stuck attitude thruster then caused a violent tumble; Armstrong undocked and used the reentry-control system to recover, forcing an emergency landing after 10 h 41 m. It was Armstrong's first spaceflight.

missions/earth/inspiration4.json.payload: ~12000 kg LEO; 4 crew, no professional astronauts
missions/earth/inspiration4.json.first: First all-civilian orbital spaceflight; raised $243M for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital
missions/earth/inspiration4.json.description: Jared Isaacman, Sian Proctor, Hayley Arceneaux and Chris Sembroski — the first orbital flight crewed entirely by people who were not professional government astronauts. Launched 2021-09-15 00:02 UTC from LC-39A on Falcon 9 B1062 (third flight), atop Crew Dragon Resilience (C207, previously flown on Crew-1). Reached a 585 km circular orbit at 51.6° inclination — the highest crewed orbit since the Hubble servicing missions. No docking with any station; three days of free flight including the first onboard cupola (replacing the docking adapter). Splashed down off the Florida coast 2021-09-18 23:06 UTC. The mission raised over $243M for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital — Arceneaux is a former St. Jude patient and the first cancer survivor in orbit.

missions/earth/liberty-bell-7.json.name: Liberty Bell 7 / MR-4
missions/earth/liberty-bell-7.json.first: Second American suborbital flight; hatch malfunction lost the capsule (recovered 1999)
missions/earth/liberty-bell-7.json.dispatch: Liberty Bell 7 flew flawlessly and is remembered for the thirty seconds after it stopped flying. Gus Grissom's suborbital hop repeated Shepard's — proof the first flight hadn't been a fluke — but on the water the new explosive hatch fired on its own, the capsule flooded, and it sank to the floor of the Atlantic while Grissom nearly drowned in his filling suit. Whether he had bumped the trigger or it had gone off by itself was argued for the rest of his life and never settled. The flight's real lesson was quieter and more useful: the most dangerous part of a spaceflight isn't always the spaceflight.
missions/earth/liberty-bell-7.json.description: Gus Grissom's 15-min suborbital flight — second American in space, first flight to feature an explosive escape hatch. After splashdown the hatch fired prematurely, the capsule flooded, and Liberty Bell 7 sank in 4900 m of water; Grissom escaped but his suit took on water and he was nearly drowned during helicopter pickup. The cause of the hatch firing remained controversial for decades; Grissom maintained he had not bumped the firing pin. Recovered 1999-07-20 by an Oceaneering/Discovery Channel expedition, restored and now displayed at the Kansas Cosmosphere & Space Center, Hutchinson KS. The Tom Wolfe book / 1983 film The Right Stuff dramatised this flight + the hatch controversy.

missions/earth/sigma-7.json.name: Sigma 7 / MA-8
missions/earth/sigma-7.json.first: First textbook Mercury flight — 6 orbits; double Glenn / Carpenter duration
missions/earth/sigma-7.json.dispatch: After two flights that ended in scares, Sigma 7 was the one that was boring on purpose — and that was the achievement. Wally Schirra called it a textbook engineering test and flew it like one: minimal experiments, careful conservation of every kilogram of fuel and every amp of power, six orbits spent proving the spacecraft could be operated with discipline rather than wrestled. He splashed down almost on top of the recovery carrier. In a program that had been improvising under pressure, Sigma 7 showed the Americans had learned to fly the thing calmly — the prerequisite for the far longer missions ahead.
missions/earth/sigma-7.json.description: Wally Schirra's 6-orbit flight — doubled Glenn's and Carpenter's mission length. Schirra called his flight a "textbook engineering test" — minimal experimental load, focus on conserving consumables, validating the vehicle for longer duration. Flight duration 9 h 13 min; orbital parameters 161 × 283 km. Splashed down ~445 km NE of Midway in the Pacific — first Mercury flight to splash in the Pacific. Aurora 7 had used 38 kg of attitude control gas; Schirra used only 32 kg with double the flight time. Capsule Sigma 7 on display at the Astronaut Memorial Planetarium and Observatory, Cocoa FL.

missions/earth/skylab-2.json.name: Skylab 2
missions/earth/skylab-2.json.dispatch: Skylab 2 is the mission that saved America's first space station and, in doing so, proved that astronauts are repair crews as much as explorers. Skylab had reached orbit crippled — its sun shield ripped off during launch, one solar panel gone, the other jammed shut, the interior overheating toward uninhabitable. Pete Conrad's crew flew up to a station that might have been a write-off, deployed a parasol sunshade through a small airlock to cool it, and then freed the stuck panel in a dangerous, improvised spacewalk that restored its power. It was the first time a crew had rescued a failing spacecraft in orbit, and it rewrote the assumption that space hardware was disposable.
missions/earth/skylab-2.json.first: First crewed Skylab visit — repaired the damaged workshop and saved the programme
missions/earth/skylab-2.json.description: Conrad, Kerwin and Weitz — the first crew to inhabit the US Skylab space station. Launched 1973-05-25 13:00 UTC on Saturn IB (SA-206), 11 days after Skylab itself was damaged at launch (the micrometeoroid / sun shield ripped off, taking one solar wing with it and jamming the second). The crew executed a 28-day rescue: Weitz attempted (and failed) to free the jammed wing during a 38-minute stand-up EVA on day 1, then Conrad and Kerwin successfully cut the restraining strap on a 3.5-hour EVA on day 14, restoring power. Deployed a Marshall-designed parasol thermal shield through the scientific airlock to bring cabin temperatures back from 54°C to 24°C. Returned 1973-06-22 13:50 UTC; CSM-116 displayed at the National Air and Space Museum, Washington DC.

missions/earth/skylab-3.json.name: Skylab 3
missions/earth/skylab-3.json.dispatch: Skylab 3 took the endurance question and nearly doubled the answer. Where the first crew had stayed 28 days, Alan Bean's crew stayed 59 — pushing the human body further into long-duration weightlessness than anyone had gone, and returning healthier than the pessimists had feared. They logged a huge haul of solar observations from the Apollo Telescope Mount and rode out a scare when thruster leaks on their Apollo ferry briefly raised the prospect of a rescue flight. Skylab 3 is where long stays in space started to look not just survivable but routine — the quiet groundwork for every months-long station tour since.
missions/earth/skylab-3.json.first: Second Skylab crew — 59 days, deployed twin-pole solar shield to replace parasol
missions/earth/skylab-3.json.description: Bean, Garriott and Lousma — the second crew to live aboard Skylab, for 59 days 11 hours. Launched 1973-07-28 11:11 UTC on Saturn IB (SA-207). Within hours of docking the CSM service module suffered an attitude-control thruster leak — back-up CSM-119 was prepped at Cape Canaveral for a possible rescue mission, but the crew completed nominally. Garriott led 305 hours of solar observations using the Apollo Telescope Mount instruments. Three EVAs deployed a twin-pole sun shield over the original parasol, repaired the rate gyro package, and recovered film canisters from the ATM. Splashed down 1973-09-25 22:19 UTC; CSM-117 displayed at the Glenn Visitor Center, Cleveland.

missions/earth/skylab-4.json.name: Skylab 4
missions/earth/skylab-4.json.dispatch: Skylab 4 set an endurance record that stood for years — 84 days aloft — and became a landmark in something less expected: who gets to run a mission. Gerald Carr's crew arrived to a punishing schedule radioed up from the ground, fell behind, and eventually pushed back, taking an unscheduled rest period — NASA and the crew themselves later disputed how deliberate the stand-down was — and forcing mission control to negotiate a workload humans could actually sustain. They also captured the era's best observations of Comet Kohoutek. The flight is remembered both for its record and for asserting, for the first time clearly, that the people in orbit — not only the planners below — have a say in how a long mission is flown.
missions/earth/skylab-4.json.first: Longest Skylab stay — 84 days, observed Comet Kohoutek, disputed "Skylab strike" rest day
missions/earth/skylab-4.json.description: Carr, Gibson and Pogue — the final and longest Skylab crew, 84 days 1 hour, all-rookie. Launched 1973-11-16 14:01 UTC on Saturn IB (SA-208). Comprehensive Earth-resources and solar observation, including a full Comet Kohoutek campaign over December–January. The mission is best remembered for what NASA later called a 'Skylab mutiny' or 'strike' — a disputed account of a rest-day stand-down around day 42 after relentless ground-controller demands compressed every minute of waking time; NASA and the crew have stated no organised strike occurred, but the underlying timeline overload was real and led to permanent NASA reforms on crew time-line planning for long-duration missions. Splashed down 1974-02-08 15:17 UTC — the last Skylab splashdown. CSM-118 displayed at the National Museum of the US Air Force, Dayton OH.

missions/earth/soyuz-1.json.name: Soyuz 1
missions/earth/soyuz-1.json.first: First Soyuz flight — parachute failure killed Vladimir Komarov (first in-flight spaceflight death)
missions/earth/soyuz-1.json.dispatch: Soyuz 1 is the flight that killed a cosmonaut, and it should never have flown. The new Soyuz spacecraft was rushed into service under political pressure with hundreds of known unresolved faults — engineers reportedly pleaded to delay — and in orbit it began to fail: a solar panel wouldn't deploy, the attitude control fought the pilot. Vladimir Komarov flew it down anyway, and on reentry the parachutes tangled and failed. He hit the ground at full speed. It was the first death in the history of human spaceflight, and its cause was less bad luck than a program that couldn't afford to admit its machine wasn't ready — the exact failure the culture of hidden, must-succeed firsts had been building toward.
missions/earth/soyuz-1.json.description: The first crewed flight of the Soyuz spacecraft, launched 23 April 1967 with Vladimir Komarov aboard. The rushed vehicle suffered cascading failures in orbit — an undeployed solar panel, attitude-control problems — and the mission was cut short. On reentry the drogue chute deployed but the main parachute failed to open properly; the descent module struck the ground near-terminal velocity and Komarov was killed — the first in-flight fatality in spaceflight history.

missions/earth/soyuz-11.json.name: Soyuz 11
missions/earth/soyuz-11.json.first: First crew to a space station (Salyut 1); all 3 died of decompression on reentry
missions/earth/soyuz-11.json.dispatch: Soyuz 11 achieved something extraordinary and then lost its crew in the last minutes of the flight. Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov, and Viktor Patsayev became the first people to live aboard a space station, spending twenty-two days aboard Salyut 1 — and then, during reentry, a valve jolted open at the instant the modules separated and let their cabin air hiss out into space. They wore no pressure suits; there had been no room for suits when the couches were fitted for three. Within seconds, at the edge of space, all three were dead. The capsule landed itself, perfectly on target; the recovery team opened it to find the crew still strapped in their seats. They remain the only human beings to have died in space — and the price bought a rule that has held ever since: crews wear pressure suits through launch and reentry, always.
missions/earth/soyuz-11.json.description: The first crewed mission to a space station — Salyut 1 — launched 6 June 1971 with Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov, and Viktor Patsayev. The crew spent 22 days aboard Salyut 1 (total mission duration 23 days 18 hours). During reentry on 30 June a pressure-equalisation valve opened prematurely at module separation (~168 km); the cabin depressurised and the three cosmonauts, unsuited, died within seconds. The capsule landed normally. They remain the only humans to have died above the Kármán line.

missions/earth/sputnik1.json.name: Sputnik 1
missions/earth/sputnik1.json.payload: 83.6 kg polished aluminium-magnesium sphere, Ø 58 cm; two transmitters (20.005 MHz + 40.002 MHz), three silver-zinc batteries (60 W), no instruments beyond a thermometer + pressure sensor
missions/earth/sputnik1.json.first: First artificial satellite to orbit Earth — start of the Space Age
missions/earth/sputnik1.json.dispatch: Sputnik 1 did almost nothing, and that was the point. No camera, no experiment worth the name — a radio, a battery, and a polished shell chosen so the world could watch the rocket that carried it. Its whole job was to reach orbit first and be heard doing it, and for twenty-one days it was: a beep on the shortwave that anyone on Earth could tune in, and that Washington could not switch off. The machine mattered far less than the fact of it — proof, broadcast to everyone at once, that the Soviet Union had beaten the United States to orbit and flew a rocket that could reach any city on the map. It burned up over the new year. The race it started ran all the way to the Moon.
missions/earth/sputnik1.json.description: Korolev's polished aluminium sphere — 58 cm wide, 83.6 kg, two transmitters on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz — became the first human-made object to reach orbit on 1957-10-04 19:28 UTC. The 215 × 939 km, 65.1° trajectory beeped over America that night and again every 96 minutes, audible on shortwave to anyone who tuned in. Batteries depleted on 1957-10-26 (after 21 days, ~315 orbits); the satellite decayed and burned up on re-entry 1958-01-04 after roughly 1440 orbits. The flight was an OKB-1 side project: Korolev needed a lightweight payload for his still-developmental R-7 ICBM and pitched 'PS-1' (Prosteyshiy Sputnik — 'simplest satellite') to Khrushchev as a propaganda coup. It worked. The shock in Washington triggered ARPA (founded 1958-02), the National Aeronautics and Space Act (signed 1958-07), and Kennedy's Moon-landing pledge four years later. Sputnik 1 also returned the first orbital ionospheric and atmospheric-density data — engineers used the Doppler shift on the 20 / 40 MHz carriers to map air density at 215 km, work that fed into every subsequent re-entry calculation.

missions/earth/voskhod-1.json.name: Voskhod 1
missions/earth/voskhod-1.json.payload: 5320 kg launch mass; three cosmonauts (no spacesuits, no ejection seats)
missions/earth/voskhod-1.json.first: First multi-crew spaceflight — three cosmonauts in a Vostok-derived capsule
missions/earth/voskhod-1.json.dispatch: Voskhod 1 was the first flight to carry more than one person into space, and it managed it by subtraction. There was no room in the one-seat Vostok for a three-person crew, so the engineers took things out — the ejection seats that had saved every previous cosmonaut, and, because even then it was too tight, the pressure suits. Komarov, Feoktistov, and Yegorov flew for a day in shirtsleeves, with no way to escape a launch or reentry emergency and no protection if the cabin lost air. Nothing went wrong, so it looked like a triumph. It was really a bet — that the corners cut to score a first wouldn't be the ones that mattered — and it happened to win.
missions/earth/voskhod-1.json.description: First three-crew spaceflight in history. Komarov, Feoktistov and Yegorov flew 1964-10-12 to 1964-10-13 in a heavily modified Vostok capsule (designated Voskhod / 'Sunrise'). Ejection seats were removed and the cabin pressure system re-rated to allow three men to sit in shirtsleeves — a propaganda victory against the planned US Gemini two-crew flights, but a brutal compromise that left the crew with no escape capability during launch or re-entry. Cabin spacing was so tight Komarov reported he could feel Yegorov's breath on his neck for 24 hours. Landed 1964-10-13 07:47 UTC near Marevka, Kazakhstan, using the new soft-landing solid-rocket retro system because no parachute ejection was possible. While they were in orbit, Khrushchev was deposed; the crew returned to a fully different Soviet leadership.

missions/earth/voskhod-2.json.name: Voskhod 2
missions/earth/voskhod-2.json.payload: 5682 kg launch mass; Voskhod capsule + inflatable Volga airlock
missions/earth/voskhod-2.json.dispatch: Voskhod 2 achieved the first spacewalk and nearly turned it into the first death in space. Alexei Leonov floated out of an inflatable airlock into vacuum, the first human ever fully outside a spacecraft — and then his suit ballooned so stiff he couldn't bend to get back in. He had to open a valve and bleed his own air out, courting the bends, just to shrink enough to fit through the hatch. It wasn't over: the automatic reentry failed, the crew flew down by hand, and they landed hundreds of kilometres off course in the frozen Siberian forest, where they waited out two nights among wolves before rescuers reached them on skis. The public saw twelve triumphant minutes; how close it came stayed secret for years.
missions/earth/voskhod-2.json.description: Pavel Belyayev + Alexei Leonov's 1-day flight — first EVA in history. Leonov spent 12 min outside Voskhod 2 (1965-03-18 11:34 UTC), pressurised through an inflatable Volga airlock that Soviet engineers added because the Voskhod hull lacked the room for full depressurisation. Leonov's suit ballooned in vacuum, jamming him outside the airlock; he had to vent suit pressure to re-enter, raising decompression-sickness risk. Re-entry was equally dramatic — the automatic landing system failed, and Belyayev manually piloted the descent module to a hard landing in deep Urals snow ~390 km off-target; the crew survived two nights in the forest among wolves before rescue helicopters arrived 1965-03-21. The cabin atmosphere also became O₂-rich in orbit, after the EVA hatch failed to re-seal, briefly risking spontaneous combustion.

missions/earth/vostok-1.json.name: Vostok 1
missions/earth/vostok-1.json.payload: 4725 kg launch mass; spherical descent module + service module
missions/earth/vostok-1.json.first: First human in space; first crewed orbital flight
missions/earth/vostok-1.json.dispatch: Vostok 1 is where the space age begins with a person in it. For 108 minutes on 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin — a 27-year-old fighter pilot — became the first human being to leave the planet and orbit it, and the world woke to find the Soviet Union had done the thing everyone assumed America would do first. He had almost no control of the spacecraft; the flight was run from the ground, and he was as much passenger as pilot, sealed in a sphere built to bring him home whether he was conscious or not. It didn't matter. A human had circled the Earth and returned, and nothing about how people saw their place in the universe was quite the same afterward.
missions/earth/vostok-1.json.description: Yuri Gagarin's 108-minute single-orbit flight — the first crewed spaceflight in history, and the first human to orbit Earth. Launched 1961-04-12 06:07 UTC from Baikonur on a Vostok-K (8K72K) launcher; orbit 169 × 327 km, inclination 65°. The spherical descent module ejected Gagarin at ~7 km altitude (a fact the USSR concealed for years to claim full crewed landing under FAI rules). Gagarin parachuted to Smelovka, Saratov Oblast; the capsule landed separately and is on display at the RKK Energia Museum in Korolyov, Russia. The flight ended Korolev's decade-long missile / satellite work and triggered the U.S. crewed-spaceflight programme + Kennedy's Moon-landing pledge six weeks later.

missions/earth/vostok-2.json.name: Vostok 2
missions/earth/vostok-2.json.first: First day in space — 17 orbits over 25 hours
missions/earth/vostok-2.json.dispatch: If Gagarin proved a person could reach orbit, Vostok 2 proved a person could live there. Gherman Titov — at twenty-five, still the youngest person ever to fly in space — spent a full day aloft, seventeen orbits over twenty-five hours, long enough to eat, sleep, and discover something no one had felt before: space sickness, the nausea of an inner ear with no up or down to hold onto. He worked through it. The flight retired a genuine fear — that the body might simply fail over hours of weightlessness — and pushed the boundary from a single lap to a full day, at a stride the Americans, still flying fifteen-minute hops, couldn't answer.
missions/earth/vostok-2.json.description: Gherman Titov's 17-orbit, 25-hour flight — the second human in space and the first to spend over a day in orbit. Launched 1961-08-06 06:00 UTC from Baikonur; at 25 years 10 months Titov remained the youngest person ever launched into space until 2021 (Oliver Daemen, NS-16). Tested human reactions to prolonged microgravity — Titov reported the first case of space motion sickness, slept ~8 hours on orbit, and made the first hand-camera Earth photographs. Capsule landed near Krasny Kut, Saratov Oblast 1961-08-07 07:18 UTC after Titov ejected during descent. Service-module strap separation problem (same as Vostok 1) recurred.

missions/earth/vostok-3.json.name: Vostok 3
missions/earth/vostok-3.json.first: First dual-flight rendezvous — flew within ~6.5 km of Vostok 4
missions/earth/vostok-3.json.dispatch: Vostok 3 opened the first act of a piece of orbital theatre. A day after Andriyan Nikolayev reached orbit, Vostok 4 followed him up, and for a while the two spacecraft flew within a few kilometres of each other — the first time two crewed craft had ever been in space together. To the world it looked like a rendezvous, and the Soviets were glad to let it. In truth neither ship could maneuver; the closeness came from launching one almost into the other's path, and the gap widened steadily after. A genuine first and a bit of a magic trick at once — and a hint at the real skill, true rendezvous, that no one yet had.

Twenty-four hours after launch Vostok 4 (Popovich) joined him in orbit — the closest approach was approximately 6.5 km, though no actual rendezvous capability existed (the two capsules had no manoeuvring thrusters). The simultaneous flight was a propaganda response to US suborbital missions and to John Glenn's Friendship 7. Nikolayev landed 1962-08-15 06:52 UTC near Karaganda, Kazakh SSR, after almost 4 days in space.

missions/earth/vostok-4.json.first: Second half of first dual flight — first communications between two crewed spacecraft
missions/earth/vostok-4.json.dispatch: Vostok 4 was the answer to Vostok 3 — the second ship in the first dual flight, and the moment two humans in two separate spacecraft first spoke to each other in orbit. Pavel Popovich launched a day after Nikolayev and closed to within about six and a half kilometres, near enough to trade radio voice directly, ship to ship, rather than through the ground. Like its partner it couldn't maneuver to hold the distance, so the two drifted apart. But the image of two cosmonauts circling the Earth in formation, talking to each other, was exactly the kind of first the program was built to manufacture.

The two capsules came within ~6.5 km and exchanged the first voice radio communications between cosmonauts in orbit. Popovich was ordered down a day early when ground controllers misinterpreted a coded phrase about thunder as the duress code-word for early termination — the real signal was a routine weather observation. Landed 1962-08-15 06:59 UTC near Karaganda, seven minutes after Vostok 3.

missions/earth/vostok-5.json.name: Vostok 5
missions/earth/vostok-5.json.first: Longest solo Earth-orbital flight — 4 days 23 hours, 81 orbits
missions/earth/vostok-5.json.dispatch: Vostok 5 set a record that still stands. Valery Bykovsky flew nearly five days alone in orbit — eighty-one laps of the planet — which remains, six decades on, the longest solo spaceflight anyone has ever made. It was an endurance test above all, pushing a single cosmonaut and a small spacecraft far past the day Titov managed, to see whether a person could simply keep going. He could. And Bykovsky wasn't even the headline of his own mission: two days into his flight, Vostok 6 went up carrying the first woman in space, and the world's attention went with her.

Launched 1963-06-14 11:59 UTC; flew the second half of his mission alongside Vostok 6 (Tereshkova, launched 2 days later). Bykovsky's planned 8-day duration was shortened due to solar-flare radiation concerns and a slow orbital decay. Landed 1963-06-19 11:06 UTC near Karaganda after parachute separation.

missions/earth/vostok-6.json.name: Vostok 6
missions/earth/vostok-6.json.first: First woman in space — Valentina Tereshkova, 48 orbits
missions/earth/vostok-6.json.dispatch: Vostok 6 carried Valentina Tereshkova, and made her the first woman in space — a fact that stood alone for nineteen years and went unmatched by the United States until 1983. She was not a pilot but a textile worker and amateur parachutist, chosen in part for exactly that symbolism: proof, the Soviet program said, that in the workers' state even the frontier of space was open to anyone. Whatever the motive, forty-eight orbits later the milestone was real and permanent, and it would be two decades before any other nation could say it had done the same.
missions/earth/vostok-6.json.description: Valentina Tereshkova's 48-orbit, 2-day-23-hour flight — the first woman in space, and still the only woman ever to have flown a solo space mission. Selected from a group of five female cosmonaut candidates assembled in 1962, Tereshkova launched 1963-06-16 09:30 UTC, only 2 years after Gagarin's first orbital flight. Her capsule programmed for an upward-rather-than-downward orbit-correction burn — she manually identified the error and ground controllers re-uploaded corrected attitude software the next day. Landed 1963-06-19 08:20 UTC near Bayevo, Altai Krai. Tereshkova later became a senior figure in Soviet politics and remains the youngest woman ever flown to orbit at 26 years.
