events.note: 2033-03. Mission climax: 113-km + 104-km binary Trojan.

missions/itokawa/hayabusa1.json.name: Hayabusa
missions/itokawa/hayabusa1.json.payload: 510 kg (incl. 60 kg of xenon for four μ10 ion thrusters)
missions/itokawa/hayabusa1.json.first: First asteroid sample ever returned to Earth (~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust, sub-milligram total)
missions/itokawa/hayabusa1.json.description: JAXA's Hayabusa (Japanese for 'falcon') flew the most heroic mission-save in spaceflight history. Launched 2003-05-09 on an M-V-5 with four μ10 ion thrusters — the most powerful ion-propulsion subsystem flown to that point. Arrived at 25143 Itokawa 2005-09-12 — a 540×270×210-m rubble-pile near-Earth asteroid. Two touchdowns (2005-11-20 + 25), both with sample-collection projectile failures, though regolith was kicked into the collection horn anyway. Then a hydrazine leak crippled attitude control, two of its three reaction wheels failed, communications lost for seven weeks, the Earth-return window slipped by three years. Engineers assembled a single working ion engine from the surviving halves of two damaged engines and nursed Hayabusa back to Earth. Sample capsule recovered at Woomera AUS 2010-06-13 returned ~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust (sub-milligram total) — confirming the asteroid's S-type composition and rubble-pile structure, and proving that asteroid sample return was possible.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: M-V-5 from Uchinoura Space Center.

events.label: ITOKAWA ARRIVAL
events.note: 2005-09-12. Station-keep at 7-km gate position.

events.label: TOUCHDOWNS
events.note: Two surface contacts 2005-11-20 + 25. Sample-collection projectiles fail to fire on command.

events.label: RECOVERY ATTEMPT
events.note: Hydrazine leak, 2 reaction wheels dead, comms lost 7 weeks.

events.label: ION ENGINE FRANKENSTEIN
events.note: One working engine assembled from surviving halves of two damaged ones.

events.label: SAMPLE RETURN
events.note: 2010-06-13. ~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust (sub-milligram total) recovered at Woomera. First asteroid sample ever returned.

missions/jupiter/europa-clipper.json.name: Europa Clipper
missions/jupiter/europa-clipper.json.payload: 6065 kg (largest planetary mission spacecraft ever launched; 100-m² solar arrays for outer-system power)
missions/jupiter/europa-clipper.json.first: First mission dedicated to characterising the habitability of an icy moon; largest planetary mission spacecraft ever launched (6065 kg, 100-m² solar arrays)
missions/jupiter/europa-clipper.json.description: Europa Clipper goes to Jupiter to study Europa — a 3,121-km icy moon believed to harbour a global liquid-water ocean beneath a 15-25 km ice shell, the most accessible potentially-habitable environment in the solar system. Launched 2024-10-14 on a Falcon Heavy at C3 41.7. A Mars gravity assist in March 2025 bent the trajectory toward Earth; an Earth gravity assist 2026-12 delivers the final push outward; arrives Jupiter 2030-04-11 for orbit insertion. The orbital tour executes 49 close Europa flybys over four years — passing within 25 km of Europa's surface on the closest passes, designed to map the entire moon while limiting the spacecraft's dose in Jupiter's brutal radiation belts. Instruments: REASON ice-penetrating radar, MASPEX mass spectrometer (samples plume material if any), E-THEMIS thermal imager (finds active geysers), magnetometer + plasma instruments confirm ocean depth from induced magnetic response.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Falcon Heavy from Kennedy LC-39A.

events.label: MARS GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: 2025-03-01. Bends trajectory toward Earth re-encounter.

events.label: EARTH GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: 2026-12-03. Final acceleration outbound to Jupiter.

events.label: JUPITER APPROACH
events.note: 2030-04-11. Final approach to JOI.

events.label: JUPITER ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: 760 m/s burn. 49 Europa flybys over 4 years follow.

missions/jupiter/galileo.json.name: Galileo
missions/jupiter/galileo.json.payload: Galileo probe and atmospheric entry probe; ~2.5 t dry mass
missions/jupiter/galileo.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit Jupiter; atmospheric probe into Jupiter clouds
missions/jupiter/galileo.json.dispatch: Galileo should have been crippled before it even arrived. Its main antenna stuck half-open on the way to Jupiter, cutting its data rate to a trickle — and the mission succeeded anyway, because engineers rewrote its software from Earth to squeeze the science through a tiny backup antenna. It became the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, dropped a probe into the giant planet’s clouds, and spent eight years touring the moons. Its greatest find emerged slowly from that persistence: the way Jupiter’s magnetic field wrapped around Europa could only be explained by a salty ocean beneath the ice — the strongest case yet that a moon of Jupiter might hold liquid water, and life. At the end it was flown into Jupiter on purpose, so it could never fall onto Europa and contaminate it.
missions/jupiter/galileo.json.description: Launched from Space Shuttle Atlantis after the long post-Challenger pause, Galileo braved the inner asteroid belt and conducted the first long-term study of Jupiter and its moons from orbit. It discovered Europa's induced magnetic field — strong evidence of a subsurface ocean — and watched Shoemaker-Levy 9 slam into Jupiter. The mission ended with a controlled plunge into Jupiter in 2003 to avoid contaminating icy moons that might harbour conditions for life.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: STS-34 deploys Galileo and an inertial upper stage from Atlantis.

events.label: JUPITER ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Main engine burn captures Galileo into orbit; an 8-year tour of moon science begins.

missions/jupiter/juice.json.name: JUICE
missions/jupiter/juice.json.payload: 6000 kg wet (2900 kg dry) — largest interplanetary spacecraft Europe has ever built. 10 instruments: JANUS (visible), MAJIS (IR), UVS, SWI (sub-mm), GALA (laser altimeter), RIME (radar sounder, NASA), J-MAG (mag), PEP (particle), RPWI (plasma waves), 3GM (radio science). 85 m² solar arrays sized for ~5.5 AU operation.
missions/jupiter/juice.json.delta_v: ~3.0 km/s (gravity-assist sequence + Jupiter orbit insertion + Ganymede orbit insertion)
missions/jupiter/juice.json.first: Largest interplanetary spacecraft built in Europe; first spacecraft ever to orbit a moon of another planet (Ganymede, 2034)
missions/jupiter/juice.json.description: JUpiter ICy moons Explorer — ESA's L-class flagship, launched 2023-04-14. The 8-year cruise uses one of the most complex gravity-assist sequences ever flown: a first-of-kind Lunar-Earth Gravity Assist on 2024-08-19, Venus 2025-08-31, then two more Earth passes in 2026 and 2029. Jupiter orbit insertion is set for 2031-07-21. After 35 close flybys of Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto over 3.5 years, JUICE will manoeuvre into a dedicated Ganymede orbit on 2034-12-31 — the first spacecraft ever to orbit a moon of another planet. Mission ends 2035 by impact on Ganymede. Primary science: existence + properties of subsurface oceans across the icy Galilean moons, ice-shell composition + tidal heating, and Jovian magnetospheric structure.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Ariane 5 ECA lifts JUICE from Kourou.

events.label: LUNAR-EARTH FLYBY
events.note: First-ever Lunar-Earth Gravity Assist manoeuvre — Moon + Earth in one swing.

events.label: VENUS FLYBY
events.note: Venus gravity assist en route back to two more Earth passes.

events.label: JUPITER ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Main engine burn places JUICE into Jupiter orbit for the icy-moons tour.

missions/jupiter/juno.json.name: Juno
missions/jupiter/juno.json.payload: Polar Jupiter orbiter; first solar-powered spacecraft to operate beyond the asteroid belt (~50 m² triple-junction solar arrays delivering ~14 kW at Earth, ~500 W at Jupiter)
missions/jupiter/juno.json.first: First polar orbiter of Jupiter; solar-powered beyond the asteroid belt for the first time
missions/jupiter/juno.json.description: Juno entered Jupiter orbit 2016-07-05 on a highly elliptical 53-day polar trajectory that takes it from inside the radiation belts (perijove ~4200 km above cloud tops) out past Callisto. Solar-powered — its ~50 m² triple-junction arrays deliver 14 kW at Earth but only ~500 W at Jupiter, the first time solar power has been used at that distance. Confirmed Jupiter has a diluted rocky core (not a sharp boundary), measured the polar cyclone arrangement (eight circumpolar storms around each pole), and imaged Io’s volcanism at unprecedented detail in 2023. Extended mission includes flybys of all four Galilean moons through 2025.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 551 lifts Juno from Cape Canaveral.

events.label: EARTH GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: Slingshot raises heliocentric energy enough to reach Jupiter.

events.label: JUPITER ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: 35-minute main-engine burn places Juno into polar Jupiter orbit.

missions/jupiter/pioneer-10.json.name: Pioneer 10
missions/jupiter/pioneer-10.json.payload: Outer-system flyby spacecraft; first to use SNAP-19 RTGs; ~155 W at launch (decaying to ~65 W of usable power; signal lost 2003)
missions/jupiter/pioneer-10.json.first: First spacecraft through the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter (1973-12-04)
missions/jupiter/pioneer-10.json.dispatch: Pioneer 10 went first, into two dangers nobody had measured. No spacecraft had crossed the asteroid belt — thought to be a shooting gallery of debris — or survived Jupiter’s radiation, believed lethal to electronics. Pioneer 10 did both: it crossed the belt unharmed (the belt, it turned out, is mostly empty), reached Jupiter in December 1973 as the first spacecraft ever to do so, and returned the first close images of the giant planet. Then it became the first human-made object aimed out of the solar system for good. Its value was proof — it turned the unknown hazards on the road to the outer planets into known ones, so the Voyagers could be built to face them.
missions/jupiter/pioneer-10.json.description: Pioneer 10 was the trail-blazer — first to cross the asteroid belt (which we then learned was much less hazardous than predicted), first to image Jupiter at close range, first to reach a heliocentric distance greater than Pluto’s perihelion (1983). It carries the Pioneer plaque designed by Carl Sagan, Frank Drake, and Linda Salzman Sagan — humanity’s first deliberate interstellar message. Final successful contact 2003-01-23 from ~82 AU; the spacecraft now drifts toward the constellation Taurus, with an encounter near Aldebaran in roughly two million years.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas-Centaur lifts Pioneer 10 on a direct ascent to Jupiter.

events.label: JUPITER CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: Flyby at ~132,000 km — first close-range photographs of the planet.

missions/mars/curiosity.json.name: Curiosity
missions/mars/curiosity.json.payload: 3839 kg launch mass (899 kg rover on surface)
missions/mars/curiosity.json.first: First nuclear-powered Mars rover; first sky-crane landing
missions/mars/curiosity.json.dispatch: Curiosity is a nuclear-powered laboratory the size of a small car, and getting it down was the hard part. Too heavy for airbags, it was lowered onto Mars in 2012 by a rocket-powered sky crane in a sequence so risky its planners called it seven minutes of terror — and it worked on the first try. Since then it has drilled its way across Gale Crater and answered the question it was sent to ask: the crater once held a lake, with the chemistry a living thing could have used. Mars had been habitable. Curiosity is still driving, climbing a mountain of layered rock that reads like the planet’s own history book.
missions/mars/curiosity.json.description: The flagship mission that defined modern Mars exploration. Curiosity is car-sized, plutonium-powered, and has driven 36+ km across Gale Crater since landing in 2012. Its instruments confirmed Mars once had habitable conditions — flowing water, complex organics, the chemistry life would need. The 'seven minutes of terror' EDL sequence, ending with a sky-crane lowering the rover on cables, is now NASA's standard for delivering large payloads to Mars surface.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 541 lifts off from Cape Canaveral SLC-41.

events.label: TMI BURN
events.note: Trans-Mars injection (3.61 km/s ∆v) sends MSL onto a heliocentric Mars-bound trajectory.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: TCM-3
events.note: Final pre-EDL correction; trajectory targets Gale Crater landing ellipse.

events.label: EDL — SEVEN MINUTES OF TERROR
events.note: Atmospheric entry, supersonic parachute, sky-crane retro-rockets, rover lowered on cables.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Curiosity arrives at Aeolis Palus, Gale Crater, 2012-08-06 05:17:57 UTC.

events.label: FIRST IMAGES
events.note: Hazcam returns first low-resolution image of the surface.

missions/mars/hope-probe.json.name: Hope Probe
missions/mars/hope-probe.json.description: The Emirates Mars Mission — Al Amal, 'Hope' — was conceived in 2014 to mark the 50th anniversary of UAE federation in 2021. The MBRSC team partnered with the University of Colorado, Arizona State, and UC Berkeley to design and integrate the spacecraft, but built it themselves. The science orbit (55-hour period, ~20,000 km × 43,000 km) covers all longitudes and times of day, capturing weather patterns no other Mars orbiter can resolve. The mission succeeded on the first attempt, making the UAE the fifth agency at Mars.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: H-IIA 202 from Tanegashima — Mitsubishi Heavy Industries provided the launch.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: MARS ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: 27-minute thruster burn captures Hope into Mars orbit 2021-02-09.

events.label: SCIENCE ORBIT
events.note: Trim manoeuvres place Hope into its 55-hour science orbit.

missions/mars/insight.json.name: InSight
missions/mars/insight.json.first: First seismometer on Mars; first interplanetary launch from US West Coast
missions/mars/insight.json.description: InSight gave Mars its first stethoscope. Its seismometer, deployed by a robotic arm onto the regolith, recorded over 1,300 marsquakes — including a magnitude-5 in 2022, the largest ever detected on another planet. The data revealed Mars's interior structure: a 1,800-km-radius molten core, a thick crust, and surprising mantle layering. The mole heat-flow experiment failed when the regolith proved too cohesive for its self-hammering design. The mission ended when dust accumulation on solar panels reduced power below operational threshold.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 401 from Vandenberg AFB — first interplanetary mission ever launched from the US West Coast.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: EDL
events.note: Atmospheric entry, parachute, terminal-descent rocket landing at Elysium Planitia.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lander arrives 2018-11-26 19:54 UTC.

events.label: SEISMOMETER DEPLOYED
events.note: Robotic arm places SEIS instrument on the surface and shields it from wind.

events.label: MISSION END
events.note: Final low-power transmission 2022-12-15. Solar panels too dust-covered to recharge.

missions/mars/mangalyaan.json.name: Mangalyaan
missions/mars/mangalyaan.json.first: First Asian Mars mission; first Mars success on first attempt
missions/mars/mangalyaan.json.description: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission cost $74 million — less than the budget of the film Gravity ($100M), and a fraction of NASA's MAVEN ($671M) which arrived two days earlier. Built in 18 months as a technology demonstrator, Mangalyaan succeeded at every objective: trans-Mars injection, deep-space navigation, Mars orbit insertion, and 8 years of science return. India became the fourth space agency at Mars and the first to succeed on its first try.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: PSLV-XL (C25) from Sriharikota — a relatively small launcher requiring orbit-raising loop.

events.label: PERIGEE BURN 1
events.note: First of six Earth orbit raising burns before trans-Mars injection.

events.label: TRANS-MARS INJECTION
events.note: Final perigee burn places spacecraft on Mars trajectory.

events.label: MARS ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Liquid Apogee Motor fires after ~10 months dormant — fired for 24 minutes to capture into orbit.

events.label: MISSION END
events.note: Lost contact 2022-04 after spacecraft propellant exhausted.

missions/mars/mariner4.json.name: Mariner 4
missions/mars/mariner4.json.first: First spacecraft to reach Mars and return close-up images of another planet
missions/mars/mariner4.json.description: The mission that ended dreams of a habitable Mars. Mariner 4's 22 grainy images, taken during a 25-minute closest approach at 9,846 km altitude, showed a cratered surface resembling the Moon — no canals, no vegetation, no obvious life. The atmosphere was 100× thinner than expected. The discovery reshaped Mars in the public imagination from sister-Earth to dead world. Tracking the spacecraft also produced the first measurement of the solar wind's structure between planets.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas LV-3 Agena-D lifts off from Cape Canaveral LC-12.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction completed; trajectory locked.

events.label: MARS FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach 9,846 km. 22 images returned over 8 hours during data playback.

events.label: FIRST IMAGES
events.note: First close-up images of another planet ever returned to Earth.

missions/mars/mariner9.json.name: Mariner 9
missions/mars/mariner9.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit another planet
missions/mars/mariner9.json.description: Mariner 9 made every orbiter that followed possible. After a 15-minute MOI burn placed it into Mars orbit on 1971-11-14, the planet below was unrecognisable — a global dust storm had hidden everything except the four Tharsis volcano summits. JPL waited it out. Through January 1972 the dust settled and Mariner 9 returned 7,329 images covering ~85% of the Martian surface, revealing Olympus Mons (the largest volcano in the solar system), Valles Marineris (the canyon system that bears its name), dried river channels suggesting an ancient liquid era, and the first close-ups of Phobos and Deimos. The mission ended 1972-10-27 when attitude-control gas ran out; the spacecraft remains in orbit, slowly decaying.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas SLV-3C / Centaur from Cape Canaveral LC-36B.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: TCM-2
events.note: Approach trim pin-targets the MOI periapsis.

events.label: MOI
events.note: 15-min solid-motor burn places Mariner 9 into a 1398 × 17,917 km, 64.4° orbit — first ever orbit of another planet.

events.label: DUST CLEARS
events.note: Global storm subsides; imaging begins.

events.label: END OF MISSION
events.note: 1972-10-27. Attitude-control gas exhausted.

missions/mars/mars-express.json.name: Mars Express
missions/mars/mars-express.json.payload: 1183 kg (1123 kg orbiter + 60 kg Beagle 2 lander)
missions/mars/mars-express.json.first: Europe's first interplanetary mission; longest-running non-NASA Mars orbiter
missions/mars/mars-express.json.description: ESA's first mission to a planet other than Earth. The orbiter has produced the longest continuous record of Mars's atmosphere, mapping water ice deposits, methane plumes, and the planet's three-dimensional weather. Beagle 2, the British-built lander it carried, reached the surface but never deployed solar panels fully — declared lost in 2004, found intact by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in 2015. The orbiter is in its third decade of operation.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Soyuz-FG / Fregat from Baikonur.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: BEAGLE 2 RELEASE
events.note: Lander separates from orbiter for independent descent.

events.label: MARS ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: 37-minute main engine burn captures orbiter into Mars orbit on Christmas Day 2003.

events.label: BEAGLE 2 SILENT
events.note: Expected first signal not received; lander declared lost.

missions/mars/mars-pathfinder.json.name: Mars Pathfinder
missions/mars/mars-pathfinder.json.first: First wheels on Mars; demonstrated airbag landing
missions/mars/mars-pathfinder.json.dispatch: Mars Pathfinder was NASA’s proof that landing on Mars did not have to cost a fortune. Instead of the retrorocket hover the Vikings used, it hit the atmosphere behind a heat shield, popped a parachute, inflated a cocoon of airbags, and bounced dozens of times across the surface before rolling to a stop and opening like a flower. Out drove Sojourner — a rover the size of a microwave, the first wheels ever to turn on another planet. The science was modest; the point was the method. The airbag landing and the faster-cheaper-better approach it proved became the template for the far more ambitious rovers — Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity — that followed.
missions/mars/mars-pathfinder.json.description: The mission that proved cheap interplanetary missions could work. Pathfinder used a novel airbag landing system — bouncing dozens of times across the surface before coming to rest — and delivered Sojourner, the first rover to operate on another planet. Sojourner traversed 100 m, examined a dozen rocks, and worked far past its 8-sol design lifetime. Pathfinder operated for 2 months 27 days; the mission's success revived NASA's interplanetary programme after the failures of the 1990s.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Delta II 7925 from Cape Canaveral.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First trajectory correction.

events.label: EDL
events.note: Direct atmospheric entry — no orbit insertion. Heat shield, parachute, retro-rockets, then airbag inflation.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lander bounces 15 times across Ares Vallis before coming to rest.

events.label: SOJOURNER DEPLOYED
events.note: First wheels on another planet.

missions/mars/mars3.json.name: Mars 3
missions/mars/mars3.json.first: First spacecraft to soft-land on Mars
missions/mars/mars3.json.description: The Soviet Union's audacious double-mission to Mars in 1971 — Mars 2 and Mars 3 launched 9 days apart. Mars 2's lander crashed; Mars 3's lander achieved the first soft-landing on Mars but went silent ~110 seconds after touchdown — the actual transmission lasted only ~14.5 seconds — possibly due to the global dust storm raging at the time. The orbiter operated for 8 months, returning dozens of images and atmospheric measurements. Despite the brief surface mission, Mars 3 demonstrated that the descent and landing problem on Mars was solvable.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K with Blok-D upper stage from Baikonur.

events.label: ORBITER MOI
events.note: Orbiter captures into Mars orbit during global dust storm.

events.label: LANDER SEPARATION
events.note: Lander separates and begins atmospheric entry.

events.label: SURFACE CONTACT
events.note: First soft-landing on Mars; transmission begins.

events.label: SIGNAL LOSS
events.note: Signal lost ~110 s after touchdown (transmission lasted ~14.5 s). Cause unconfirmed; dust storm leading suspect.

missions/mars/maven.json.name: MAVEN
missions/mars/maven.json.first: First mission dedicated to studying how Mars lost its atmosphere
missions/mars/maven.json.description: MAVEN — Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution — answers the question 'where did Mars's air go?' Its elliptical orbit dips into the upper atmosphere, sampling ions and neutrals as the solar wind strips them away. Findings: Mars loses about 100 g of atmosphere per second to space — over billions of years that's enough to explain the missing climate. The spacecraft also serves as a critical relay for surface assets, including Curiosity and Perseverance.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas V 401 from Cape Canaveral SLC-41.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First trajectory correction.

events.label: MARS ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: 33-minute main engine burn captures MAVEN into a 35-hour elliptical science orbit.

events.label: FIRST SCIENCE
events.note: Begins atmosphere-sampling 'deep dip' campaigns to periapsis altitudes ~125 km.

missions/mars/mmx.json.name: MMX
missions/mars/mmx.json.first: First sample return from a Martian moon
missions/mars/mmx.json.description: Martian Moons eXploration is JAXA's plan to land on Phobos, scoop ~10 g of regolith, and bring it home. The samples may settle a long-debated question: are Phobos and Deimos captured asteroids, or fragments from an ancient impact on Mars itself? The mission also includes a German-French rover for Phobos surface mobility — a wholly different operations model from anything the Hayabusa missions did at Itokawa or Ryugu. Launch was planned for 2024 but slipped to 2026 due to delays in JAXA's H3 launch vehicle.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: H3-24L from Tanegashima — JAXA's new heavy lifter.

events.label: MARS ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Capture into Mars orbit; transfer to Phobos quasi-orbit over following months.

events.label: ROVER DEPLOY
events.note: DLR/CNES rover (~25 kg) released onto Phobos surface for in-situ studies.

events.label: PHOBOS SAMPLE
events.note: MMX touches down on Phobos; ~10 g of regolith collected.

events.label: EARTH RETURN
events.note: Sample re-entry capsule arrives at Earth ~2031.

missions/mars/opportunity.json.name: Opportunity
missions/mars/opportunity.json.payload: 1063 kg (cruise stage + EDL + rover); 174 kg surface mass
missions/mars/opportunity.json.first: Longest-driving Mars rover (45.16 km); 14-year surface lifetime against a 90-sol design
missions/mars/opportunity.json.dispatch: Opportunity drove a marathon across another planet. Spirit’s twin, landed in 2004 for a ninety-day mission, it worked for fourteen years and crossed more than forty-five kilometres — the longest distance any vehicle has travelled on any world. It came down, by luck, in a small crater whose walls exposed exactly the water-laid rock it was sent to find, and then it just kept going, crater to crater, reading the ancient water story of Mars mile after mile. A planet-wide dust storm finally silenced it in 2018.
missions/mars/opportunity.json.description: Opportunity (MER-B) hit a planetary jackpot — its airbag-cocooned lander bounced 26 times across Meridiani Planum and rolled into a 22-m crater (Eagle) by sheer luck, surrounded by exposed bedrock a rover could read without driving. First images showed jarosite + "blueberry" hematite concretions, the strongest mineral evidence to that point of standing liquid water on early Mars. Over 14 years 138 days (5,111 sols) Opportunity traversed 45.16 km — the Mars rover marathon record — visiting Endurance, Victoria, and Endeavour craters. A planet-wide dust storm in June 2018 blocked sunlight from its solar panels; final transmission was 2018-06-10, and NASA declared end-of-mission 2019-02-13.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Delta II 7925H Heavy from Cape Canaveral LC-17B.

events.label: TCM-1
events.note: First mid-course correction.

events.label: TCM-4
events.note: Final pre-EDL trim.

events.label: EDL
events.note: Heat shield, parachute, retro-rockets, airbags.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN — INTO EAGLE CRATER
events.note: Bounced 26 times. Rolled into a 22-m crater by chance, surrounded by exposed bedrock.

events.label: FINAL TRANSMISSION
events.note: 2018-06-10. Planet-wide dust storm cuts solar power.

events.label: MISSION END
events.note: NASA declares end-of-mission 2019-02-13. 45.16 km traversed.

missions/mars/perseverance.json.name: Perseverance
missions/mars/perseverance.json.payload: 3839 kg launch mass (1025 kg rover; 1.8 kg Ingenuity helicopter)
missions/mars/perseverance.json.first: First helicopter on another planet (Ingenuity); first sample caching for Mars Sample Return
missions/mars/perseverance.json.dispatch: Perseverance went to Mars to look for the dead. Landed in 2021 on the floor of Jezero Crater — a basin holding the delta of a river that fed a lake billions of years ago, exactly the kind of place life would have left traces — it is the first rover built specifically to search for signs of ancient life, and to do something no mission had done: seal Martian rock into tubes and set them aside for a future spacecraft to carry home. It also delivered Ingenuity, the small helicopter that made the first powered flight on another planet. If the samples it is caching are ever returned, they will be the first pieces of another planet’s surface brought back to Earth.
missions/mars/perseverance.json.description: Perseverance is the most ambitious Mars surface mission ever flown. Mars Sample Return depends on it — the rover is collecting and caching samples in tubes that a future mission will retrieve and bring to Earth. Ingenuity, the first helicopter on another planet, flew 72 missions before retiring with damaged rotors in January 2024 — proving controlled flight is possible in Mars's thin atmosphere. MOXIE, an oxygen-from-CO2 demonstrator, produced the first locally-made oxygen on another planet, a rehearsal for crewed Mars missions.

events.label: LAUNCH

missions/mars/phoenix.json.name: Phoenix
missions/mars/phoenix.json.payload: 670 kg launch mass (350 kg landed mass)
missions/mars/phoenix.json.first: First confirmation of water ice in the Martian arctic regolith; first soft propulsive Mars landing since Viking 2
missions/mars/phoenix.json.description: Phoenix was salvaged from the cancelled Mars Surveyor 2001 program — flight hardware in storage for six years, reassembled and retargeted to the Martian north polar plains. The name was chosen literally. Landed 2008-05-25 at 68.22°N, 234.25°E on Vastitas Borealis, further north than any prior surface mission. Within days the robotic arm scraped through topsoil and exposed bright white ice that visibly sublimated on camera over four sols — direct confirmation of subsurface water ice in the Martian arctic. Detected perchlorates in the regolith and observed snow falling from clouds. Mission ended 2008-11-02 as solar power fell below operational threshold at the onset of Mars winter; the lander was never expected to survive the polar night.

missions/mars/schiaparelli.json.name: Schiaparelli EDM
missions/mars/schiaparelli.json.payload: 577 kg (EDM lander part of ExoMars 2016 mission with Trace Gas Orbiter)
missions/mars/schiaparelli.json.first: ESA's first Mars surface attempt; intended to demonstrate EDL ahead of ExoMars Rosalind Franklin
missions/mars/schiaparelli.json.description: Schiaparelli was the entry-descent-landing demonstrator carried piggyback on the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO). Named for the Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli, the craft was built to prove the EDL stack ESA intended to scale up for the Rosalind Franklin rover. Schiaparelli separated from TGO on 16 October 2016 and entered the Martian atmosphere three days later. The descent profile collapsed: a saturated inertial measurement unit caused the navigation software to think the craft had already landed at altitude — the parachute jettisoned early and the braking thrusters cut off after firing for only 3 seconds. Schiaparelli struck the surface at ~150 m/s. TGO itself completed orbit insertion successfully and continues operating.

missions/mars/spirit.json.name: Spirit
missions/mars/spirit.json.payload: 1063 kg (cruise stage + EDL + rover); 174 kg surface mass
missions/mars/spirit.json.first: First of the Mars Exploration Rover twins; longest-lived rover until passed by Curiosity
missions/mars/spirit.json.dispatch: Spirit was built for ninety days and worked for six years. One of a pair of golf-cart-sized geologists landed in 2004, it was sent to read the rocks for evidence of a wetter Martian past — and it found it, uncovering minerals that only form in water and, in one place, silica deposits like those left by hot springs on Earth. It climbed hills no one had planned for it to reach and survived winters it was never designed to see, until a wheel failed and it bogged down in soft sand. It kept transmitting from where it was stuck until the Martian cold finally took it.
missions/mars/spirit.json.description: Spirit (MER-A) bounced 28 times across the floor of Gusev Crater on 2004-01-04 and rolled to a stop 250 m from its first impact. Designed for a 90-sol primary mission, it would survive 2,208 sols. Drove 7.7 km across Gusev's plains, climbed the Columbia Hills, and uncovered hematite-bearing rocks that signalled persistent ancient water. In 2009-04 a wheel broke through a sulphate crust at "Troy" and Spirit ground to a halt in soft soil; the team converted it to a stationary platform. Final transmission 2010-03-22; mission declared ended 2011-05-25. Twinned with Opportunity, which landed three weeks later on the opposite side of Mars.

missions/mars/starship-demo.json.name: Starship Demo
missions/mars/starship-demo.json.vehicle: Starship (Super Heavy + Starship upper stage, expended)
missions/mars/starship-demo.json.first: First fully reusable launch system to attempt Mars landing
missions/mars/starship-demo.json.description: An uncrewed demonstration of the Starship Mars architecture: launch on Super Heavy, refill in LEO from a tanker variant, then trans-Mars injection of a fully-fuelled Starship and powered descent to the Martian surface. SpaceX's stated target is a 2026-2027 launch window; engineering reality (Starship still working through orbital flight reliability and on-orbit refilling has not been demonstrated) makes 2028 or later more likely. If it succeeds, it inverts the Mars payload economics — from thousands of kg to one hundred tonnes per landing.

events.note: Starship from Boca Chica or Cape Canaveral — first super-heavy interplanetary launch.

events.label: ORBITAL REFILLING

missions/mars/starship-mars-crew.json.name: Starship Mars Crew
missions/mars/starship-mars-crew.json.vehicle: Starship (Super Heavy + Starship + on-orbit refilling tanker fleet)
missions/mars/starship-mars-crew.json.payload: Crew of ~10 + ISRU equipment + return propellant production hardware
missions/mars/starship-mars-crew.json.delta_v: ~21 km/s (round trip with Mars surface refuelling)
missions/mars/starship-mars-crew.json.first: First proposed crewed return mission to Mars (SpaceX architecture)
missions/mars/starship-mars-crew.json.description: SpaceX's long-term crewed Mars architecture as outlined in Elon Musk's 2016, 2017, and 2024 IAC presentations. A Starship lifts off from Earth fully fuelled in low-Earth orbit via a fleet of refilling tanker flights, performs trans-Mars injection, and lands a crew of roughly 10 with cargo and ISRU equipment on the Martian surface. Return-leg propellant (methane + liquid oxygen) is manufactured on Mars from atmospheric CO₂ and subsurface water ice via the Sabatier process, enabling the same Starship to lift off again, perform trans-Earth injection, and return the crew. Round-trip duration depends on the launch window and surface stay; the illustrative timeline shown here is ~2.5 years door-to-door (213 days outbound, ~500-day surface stay, return on the next favourable window). The architecture is conceptual — date and parameters subject to substantial revision pending Starship maturation and ISRU validation.

missions/mars/tianwen1.json.name: Tianwen-1
missions/mars/tianwen1.json.first: First mission to deliver orbiter, lander, and rover to Mars in a single launch
missions/mars/tianwen1.json.description: China's first Mars mission accomplished what no agency had ever attempted in one launch: orbital insertion, atmospheric entry, soft landing, and rover deployment. The Zhurong rover operated 358 sols at Utopia Planitia, traversing 1.9 km, before entering planned hibernation in May 2022; it has not woken since (likely due to dust accumulation on solar panels). The orbiter remains active, mapping the planet at high resolution and serving as relay for ground assets.

missions/mars/viking1.json.name: Viking 1
missions/mars/viking1.json.first: First fully successful Mars landing; first long-duration surface science
missions/mars/viking1.json.description: The mission that gave us our first sustained look at the Martian surface. Viking 1's lander operated for 6 years 4 months at Chryse Planitia — running biology experiments designed to detect life (results ambiguous; one experiment produced a positive signal still debated decades later), measuring weather, returning panoramic images, and analysing soil composition. The Viking orbiters together mapped 97% of Mars at ~300 m resolution and helped scout landing sites for missions still decades away.

events.note: Titan IIIE-Centaur from Cape Canaveral LC-41.

events.label: MARS ORBIT INSERTION

events.label: LANDER SEPARATION
events.note: Lander detaches for descent to Chryse Planitia.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lander touches down 1976-07-20, exactly 7 years after Apollo 11.

events.label: FIRST PANORAMA
events.note: First high-resolution surface images returned.

missions/mercury/bepicolombo.json.name: BepiColombo
missions/mercury/bepicolombo.json.payload: 4100 kg launch stack: MTM (Mercury Transfer Module, ESA — 4 ion thrusters, solar arrays) + MPO (Mercury Planetary Orbiter, ESA, 1230 kg, 11 instruments) + MIO (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, JAXA, 285 kg, 5 instruments) + MOSIF sunshield. Two science orbiters separate after Mercury arrival.
missions/mercury/bepicolombo.json.first: First Europe + Japan joint planetary mission; second-ever spacecraft to orbit Mercury (after Messenger)
missions/mercury/bepicolombo.json.description: Joint ESA / JAXA mission to Mercury, launched 2018-10-20 — named after Italian mathematician Giuseppe (Bepi) Colombo, who designed Mariner 10's multi-flyby trajectory. The 8-year cruise uses 9 gravity assists (Earth 2020, Venus 2020, Venus 2021, then six Mercury flybys 2021–2025) plus continuous ion-electric thrust from the Mercury Transfer Module to bleed off the enormous solar-gravity gradient between Earth and Mercury orbits. Mercury orbit insertion 2026-11-21; science operations begin early 2027 after MTM jettison and separation of the two orbiters — ESA's MPO (planetary surface + composition) and JAXA's Mio (magnetosphere). Tests of general relativity via radio-science range tracking through Mercury's strong solar-gravity environment are also planned.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Ariane 5 ECA lifts BepiColombo from Kourou on its 8-year ion-cruise to Mercury.

events.label: EARTH FLYBY
events.note: Single Earth gravity assist begins the inner-system gravity-assist chain.

events.label: VENUS FLYBY #1
events.note: First Venus gravity assist.

events.label: VENUS FLYBY #2
events.note: Second Venus gravity assist begins the Mercury approach phase.

events.label: MERCURY FLYBY #1
events.note: First of six Mercury gravity assists.

missions/mercury/mariner10.json.name: Mariner 10
missions/mercury/mariner10.json.payload: 503 kg — TV cameras, IR + UV spectrometers, magnetometer, charged-particle telescope
missions/mercury/mariner10.json.first: First Mercury flyby; first dual-planet flyby; first gravity-assist mission
missions/mercury/mariner10.json.description: First spacecraft to visit Mercury, first to fly past two planets, and first to use a gravity assist to reach its destination. Launched 1973-11-03 05:45 UTC from Cape Canaveral LC-36B on Atlas SLV-3D Centaur AC-34. Mariner 10 swung past Venus on 1974-02-05 (5768 km closest approach, first UV cloud-belt imaging of Venus) using the encounter to drop its perihelion into Mercury's orbital realm — the first deliberate gravity-assist trajectory in space history. Made three Mercury flybys: 1974-03-29 (703 km), 1974-09-21 (48069 km), and 1975-03-16 (327 km). Imaged ~45% of Mercury's surface — the only resolved imagery available until MESSENGER (2008-2015). Discovered Mercury's intrinsic magnetic field and thin sodium-helium exosphere. Solar-array temperature management was an open mission engineering problem: project scientists tilted the panels and rolled the spacecraft to keep them under 115°C. Mission ended 1975-03-24 when attitude-control nitrogen propellant was depleted; spacecraft is presumed to be in heliocentric orbit, periodically passing Mercury.

events.note: Atlas SLV-3D Centaur AC-34 from CCAFS LC-36B 1973-11-03 05:45 UTC.

events.label: VENUS FLYBY
events.note: 5768 km closest approach 1974-02-05; first deliberate gravity-assist trajectory in space history.

events.label: MERCURY 1
events.note: 703 km closest approach 1974-03-29; first Mercury images.

events.label: MERCURY 2
events.note: 48069 km closest approach 1974-09-21; southern-hemisphere imaging.

events.label: MERCURY 3

events.label: PROPELLANT END

missions/mercury/messenger.json.name: MESSENGER
missions/mercury/messenger.json.payload: Mercury orbiter; sunshade-protected (front-side 370 °C, back-side -45 °C); seven instruments including imaging, spectrometers, magnetometer, laser altimeter
missions/mercury/messenger.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit Mercury; first complete surface map of the innermost planet
missions/mercury/messenger.json.description: MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) used six gravity assists across seven years — Earth, Venus twice, Mercury three times — to slow into Mercury orbit on 2011-03-18. Sunshade-protected with one side at 370 °C and the other at -45 °C. Discoveries included water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters, previously unknown “hollows” geological features, and confirmation that Mercury's iron core occupies ~85 % of the planet's radius (the largest core-to-radius ratio of any planet in the solar system). Mission ended with a controlled impact onto Mercury’s surface 2015-04-30 after fuel ran out.

events.note: Delta II 7925H lifts MESSENGER on a six-flyby trajectory.

events.label: EARTH GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: First of six assists to slow the trajectory enough to enter Mercury orbit.

events.label: MERCURY ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Main-engine burn places MESSENGER into Mercury orbit after seven years of cruise.

missions/moon/apollo10.json.name: Apollo 10
missions/moon/apollo10.json.payload: 42775 kg launched (CSM Charlie Brown (CSM-106) + LM Snoopy (LM-4))
missions/moon/apollo10.json.first: Full lunar-landing dress rehearsal — LM descended to ~15.6 km altitude
missions/moon/apollo10.json.dispatch: Apollo 10 flew the entire landing — right up to the last fifteen kilometres — and then, by design, turned around. Stafford and Cernan took the Lunar Module down to within a stone's throw of the surface at Tranquility, ran every step of the descent, and climbed back to orbit without touching down. NASA even left the ascent tanks half-empty, so that however tempting it got, going for it was never an option. It is the least-celebrated flight of the program and one of the most disciplined: a full-speed rehearsal by two men who flew a quarter-million miles knowing the landing belonged to someone else.
missions/moon/apollo10.json.description: The full dress rehearsal for the first lunar landing. Stafford and Cernan flew LM Snoopy down to ~15.6 km altitude above the planned Apollo 11 landing site at Mare Tranquillitatis — every step of a landing approach except the actual landing itself. They confirmed the descent profile, the landing radar, the ascent trajectory, and the rendezvous procedure that Apollo 11 would use two months later. The LM's ascent-stage propellant tanks were deliberately underfueled (~50 % of nominal) to prevent any temptation to attempt a landing. Snoopy's ascent stage was the only one to leave lunar orbit with positive ∆v — jettisoned into a heliocentric orbit where it remains today, intermittently re-detected by amateur astronomers (most recently confirmed by Nick Howes / Faulkes Telescope, 2019).

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Saturn V (AS-505) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39B 1969-05-18 16:49 UTC — first crewed launch from LC-39B.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection. S-IVB ∆v ~3.05 km/s.

events.label: LOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion. SPS ∆v ~0.91 km/s.

events.label: LM SEPARATION
events.note: Snoopy undocks from Charlie Brown. Crew of two (Stafford + Cernan) descend toward Mare Tranquillitatis.

events.label: CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: Snoopy reaches ~15.6 km above Apollo 11 target site — no landing; everything verified except touchdown itself.

events.label: ASCENT + RENDEZVOUS
events.note: Snoopy ascent stage rendezvous with Charlie Brown — first complete LM-to-CSM redocking in lunar orbit.

events.label: TEI
events.note: Trans-Earth injection. SPS ∆v ~1.0 km/s.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN

missions/moon/apollo11.json.name: Apollo 11
missions/moon/apollo11.json.first: First humans on another celestial body
missions/moon/apollo11.json.dispatch: Apollo 11 was the flight the whole program was built to make — the one that had to work. For eight years and $25 billion, everything NASA did came down, in the end, to getting two people onto this particular patch of grey dust and back off it alive. When Armstrong called "the Eagle has landed," the Cold-War race that opened with a beeping sphere over American cities was effectively over. What's easy to forget now is how little margin there was: the crew came down with seconds of fuel to spare, past a boulder field the maps hadn't shown, riding a guidance computer that was throwing alarms the whole way. It worked anyway — and for one night, a fifth of the species watched the same thing at the same time.
missions/moon/apollo11.json.description: The mission that fulfilled Kennedy's 1961 commitment to put a man on the Moon by the end of the decade. Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 hours 36 minutes on the lunar surface — 2.5 hours of EVA, 21.55 kg of samples, and a single commemorative plaque. The laser retroreflector they installed at Mare Tranquillitatis still receives pulses today, measuring the Earth-Moon distance to millimetre precision. The mission was watched live by ~600 million people, one fifth of humanity at the time.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Saturn V (AS-506) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39A 1969-07-16 13:32 UTC.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection burn — S-IVB stage propels CSM/LM toward Moon.

events.label: MOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Lunar Module Eagle lands at Mare Tranquillitatis 1969-07-20 20:17:40 UTC.

events.label: FIRST STEP
events.note: Armstrong steps onto lunar surface; 'one small step for [a] man'.

events.label: ASCENT
events.note: Eagle lifts off after 21h 36m on surface.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: CM Columbia returns crew to Pacific Ocean 1969-07-24.

missions/moon/apollo12.json.name: Apollo 12
missions/moon/apollo12.json.payload: 46782 kg launched (CSM Yankee Clipper (CSM-108) + LM Intrepid (LM-6))
missions/moon/apollo12.json.first: Second crewed Moon landing — pinpoint touchdown 163 m from Surveyor 3
missions/moon/apollo12.json.dispatch: If Apollo 11 proved you could reach the Moon, Apollo 12 proved you could reach a particular spot on it. Thirty-six seconds after launch, lightning struck the rocket and knocked the spacecraft's instruments offline; a twenty-four-year-old controller named John Aaron pulled an obscure fix — "SCE to AUX" — from memory, and the flight went on. Then Conrad and Bean set their Lunar Module down on the Ocean of Storms a few hundred feet from a probe that had been sitting there for two years, walked over, and brought pieces of it home. That precision was the real result: the Moon had stopped being a destination and become an address.
missions/moon/apollo12.json.description: The second crewed Moon landing. Saturn V was struck by lightning twice during ascent (T+36 s and T+52 s) — Bean restored the spacecraft via the famous "SCE to AUX" call from EECOM John Aaron, then the crew re-aligned the inertial measurement unit in lunar orbit. Conrad and Bean executed a pinpoint landing on the Ocean of Storms within 163 m of Surveyor 3 (which had soft-landed in April 1967), then walked to Surveyor 3 and removed its camera + sample of its surface — pieces that came home to Earth for analysis of long-term lunar-surface exposure. They deployed ALSEP (the full Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package — the first ALSEP, vs Apollo 11's simpler EASEP) which transmitted data for 8 years. The mission returned 34 kg of samples including dark mare basalts.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Saturn V (AS-507) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39A 1969-11-14 16:22 UTC. Two lightning strikes on the stack (T+36 s, T+52 s) tripped fuel cells offline; recovered via "SCE to AUX" call.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection — recovery from lightning strikes verified; mission GO for Moon.

events.label: LOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion. SPS ∆v ~0.89 km/s.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Intrepid lands at Oceanus Procellarum (Statio Cognitum) 1969-11-19 06:54 UTC — within 163 m of Surveyor 3 (the most precise lunar landing yet).

events.label: SURVEYOR 3 VISIT
events.note: Conrad + Bean walk to Surveyor 3 (~163 m away), remove its TV camera + samples for return to Earth — first time a crew visited a previously-landed robotic spacecraft.

events.label: ASCENT
events.note: Intrepid lifts off after 31 h 31 m on surface. 34 kg of samples returned.

events.label: LM IMPACT
events.note: Intrepid ascent stage deliberately crashed onto Moon to calibrate ALSEP seismometers — the first crewed-mission spacecraft stage deliberately impacted the Moon and recorded by a surface seismometer.

events.label: TEI
events.note: Trans-Earth injection. SPS ∆v ~1.0 km/s.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: CM splashed down in South Pacific 1969-11-24 20:58 UTC. Recovery by USS Hornet.

missions/moon/apollo13.json.name: Apollo 13
missions/moon/apollo13.json.first: The mission that turned a near-disaster into NASA's most celebrated rescue
missions/moon/apollo13.json.dispatch: Apollo 13 never landed, and it is the mission everyone remembers. Two days out, an oxygen tank tore itself apart and turned a routine flight to the Fra Mauro highlands into a four-day problem of keeping three men alive in a dying spacecraft a quarter-million miles from home. What saved them was not heroics; it was preparation and a roomful of people working the problem in real time, improvising a way to breathe and a way home out of whatever was already bolted to the vehicle. NASA called it a successful failure. It is closer to the truth to say it is the flight that proved the agency was as good as it claimed to be.
missions/moon/apollo13.json.description: Apollo 13 was meant to be the third crewed lunar landing, targeted at the Fra Mauro highlands. At 55 hours 54 minutes into the flight an oxygen tank in the Service Module ruptured, crippling the Command-Service Module's electrical and life-support systems. With landing scrubbed, the crew — James Lovell, Jack Swigert, and Fred Haise — powered down the CSM, moved into the Lunar Module Aquarius as a lifeboat, and used the LM's descent engine for a Pericynthion+2-hour burn that placed them on a fast free-return trajectory. They swung past the Moon at 254 km altitude on 1970-04-15 and splashed down safely in the South Pacific on 1970-04-17. The mission is studied today as a model of disciplined real-time engineering improvisation.

events.label: SATURN V LAUNCH
events.note: Liftoff from KSC LC-39A. Center engine of S-II second stage shut down two minutes early — outer engines compensated.

events.label: TLI
events.note: Trans-lunar injection burn by S-IVB; CSM + LM commit to cislunar trajectory.

events.label: MCC-2
events.note: Mid-course correction shifts the spacecraft off the free-return trajectory onto a Fra Mauro approach.

events.label: OXYGEN TANK #2 RUPTURE
events.note: SM cryo-stir command initiates a short-circuit fire and tank rupture. "Houston, we've had a problem." Power and water dwindle; LM Aquarius becomes the lifeboat.

events.label: FREE-RETURN BURN
events.note: 31-second LM descent-engine burn returns the spacecraft to a free-return trajectory.

events.label: LUNAR FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach 254 km altitude over Mare Cognitum — at 400,171 km, the farthest humans had travelled from Earth (record held 1970–2026, surpassed by Artemis II in April 2026).

events.label: PC+2 BURN
events.note: Pericynthion-plus-2-hour burn shortens the return-to-Earth time by ten hours.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: CSM re-entry and South Pacific splashdown, recovered by USS Iwo Jima.

missions/moon/apollo14.json.name: Apollo 14
missions/moon/apollo14.json.payload: 46305 kg launched (CSM Kitty Hawk (CSM-110) + LM Antares (LM-8))
missions/moon/apollo14.json.first: Third lunar landing — Apollo 13's lost target reached; Shepard's golf shots
missions/moon/apollo14.json.dispatch: Apollo 14 had to prove the program could still land. It flew nine months after Apollo 13 nearly killed its crew, took over the target Apollo 13 never reached, and put Alan Shepard back in space a decade after he became the first American to leave the planet — grounded in between for years by an inner-ear disorder, and now, at forty-seven, the oldest person to walk on the Moon. He and Mitchell came up about thirty metres short of Cone Crater's rim, unable to tell in the confusing terrain how close they had actually gotten. Then, in the last minutes on the surface, Shepard swung a makeshift six-iron at two golf balls — a stunt, and also a quiet signal that the crisis was behind them and Apollo was flying again.
missions/moon/apollo14.json.description: The third crewed Moon landing and Alan Shepard's second flight — making him both the first American in space (Freedom 7, 1961) and the fifth man on the Moon, at age 47 the oldest Moonwalker. Apollo 14 was the recovery mission after Apollo 13's aborted landing, taking over Apollo 13's intended Fra Mauro Highlands target. Shepard and Mitchell deployed ALSEP, completed two EVAs totalling 9 h 23 m, and pulled the modular equipment transporter (MET, a rickshaw-style cart — the LRV was still one mission away) toward Cone Crater, though they came up ~30 m short of the rim due to navigation uncertainty in the cratered terrain. In the final minutes of EVA-2, Shepard improvised a six-iron golf-club head onto a sample-collection handle and hit two golf balls "miles and miles and miles" (one was later analysed from imagery at ~24 m and ~37 m). Stuart Roosa carried tree seeds in Kitty Hawk that became the "Moon Trees" planted across the US. 42 kg of samples returned.

missions/moon/apollo15.json.name: Apollo 15
missions/moon/apollo15.json.first: First J-mission — extended stay, first Lunar Roving Vehicle, "Genesis Rock"
missions/moon/apollo15.json.dispatch: By Apollo 15 the race was long over, and the science took the wheel — literally. This was the first flight to carry the Lunar Rover, which turned a two-mile walking radius into a proper eighteen-mile field expedition, and it set down not on a safe flat plain but in a valley between a mountain range and a winding canyon. Scott and Irwin came home with the "Genesis Rock," a four-billion-year-old shard of the Moon's original crust that confirmed how it had formed. Apollo had stopped visiting the Moon and started studying it — and it kept getting better at that right up until it was cancelled.
missions/moon/apollo15.json.description: The first "J-mission" — extended-stay scientific Apollo with the new Lunar Roving Vehicle. The LRV gave Scott + Irwin a 27.9 km traverse range (vs the 3.5 km of walking-only Apollo 14), opening the dramatic Hadley-Apennine site at the foot of a 4.5-km mountain range and the edge of the sinuous Hadley Rille. Three EVAs totalling 18 h 35 m, 77 kg of samples returned, including the famous "Genesis Rock" (sample 15415) — a 4.1-billion-year-old anorthosite confirming the magma-ocean origin of the lunar highlands crust. Scott's televised "hammer-feather drop" verified Galileo's law of gravitation live. Worden in lunar orbit operated a SIM-bay full of remote-sensing instruments (mapping cameras, gamma-ray, X-ray, alpha-particle spectrometers) and performed the first deep-space EVA on the way home (~39-minute EVA at ~317 000 km from Earth to retrieve the film canisters). Apollo 15's recovery was marred by one of three parachutes failing to deploy — CM splashed down hard but crew was safe.

missions/moon/apollo16.json.name: Apollo 16
missions/moon/apollo16.json.first: First Moon landing in the lunar highlands — Descartes; John Young's "lunar Grand Prix"
missions/moon/apollo16.json.dispatch: Apollo 16 went to the lunar highlands to sample ancient volcanoes and found there had never been any. Geologists were sure the pale, rugged Descartes region was volcanic; every rock Young and Duke brought back was breccia — rubble welded together by impacts. Being wrong was the payoff: the Moon's bright highlands turned out to be a record of a young solar system under relentless bombardment, not eruption. It is a clean example of how exploration actually earns its keep — you go to confirm what you already think you know, and the place tells you something better.
missions/moon/apollo16.json.description: The fifth crewed Moon landing and the first to a non-mare highland site. Geologists had expected Descartes to be volcanic; Apollo 16 disproved this — every rock returned was breccia (impact-shattered debris), reshaping understanding of the lunar highlands as products of catastrophic impacts rather than ancient volcanism. Young and Duke completed three LRV-supported EVAs totalling 20 h 14 m, traversed 26.7 km, and returned 95.7 kg of samples (the heaviest Apollo haul to that date). Young's "lunar Grand Prix" — a televised speed test of the LRV — peaked at ~17 km/h. Duke's 11-second hop attempt during a long-jump record attempt put him at risk of damaging his PLSS backpack and was called off. Charlie Duke's family photo + the "Far-UV Camera/Spectrograph" — the first astronomical observatory operated from the surface of another world — both ended up at the landing site. Mattingly, originally on Apollo 13 (replaced before launch over German measles concerns), finally got to fly to the Moon.

missions/moon/apollo17.json.name: Apollo 17
missions/moon/apollo17.json.first: Last crewed mission to the Moon (and the only Apollo with a trained geologist)
missions/moon/apollo17.json.dispatch: Apollo 17 was the end, though almost no one watching in December 1972 believed it would be. It was also, belatedly, the flight that put a real scientist on the Moon — the geologist Harrison Schmitt, whose eye caught the orange volcanic glass at Shorty Crater that rewrote what the Moon is made of. Cernan and Schmitt stayed three days, drove twenty-two miles, and then Cernan climbed the ladder for the last time anyone has, saying they left "as we came, and God willing, we shall return." More than half a century later no one has — and every serious argument for going back still begins with the fact that we once could.
missions/moon/apollo17.json.description: The last time humans visited another world — over half a century ago. Cernan and Schmitt spent 75 hours on the surface, drove the LRV 35.7 km, and brought back 110.5 kg of samples. Schmitt was the only trained scientist (geologist) ever to walk on the Moon, and his findings — particularly the orange volcanic glass at Shorty Crater — reshaped lunar geology. Cernan's last words before climbing the ladder for the final time: 'We leave as we came, and God willing, we shall return.' Artemis IV is now meant to make good on that promise.

missions/moon/apollo8.json.name: Apollo 8
missions/moon/apollo8.json.first: First humans to leave low Earth orbit + orbit the Moon
missions/moon/apollo8.json.dispatch: Apollo 8 was a bet placed in a hurry. Intelligence suggested the Soviets might loop a crew around the Moon first, so in the summer of 1968 NASA tore up the flight plan and sent three men to lunar orbit on only the third launch of a rocket that had never carried a crew. It should have been reckless. Instead it became the year's one piece of good news — 1968 had been assassinations, Vietnam, cities on fire — and on Christmas Eve a billion people heard Genesis read from lunar orbit and, in Bill Anders' photograph, watched their whole world rise over a dead horizon for the first time. Apollo 11 is remembered for the Moon. Apollo 8 is the one that showed us the Earth.
missions/moon/apollo8.json.description: The first crewed mission to leave low Earth orbit, the first to escape Earth gravity, and the first to orbit the Moon. Launched 1968-12-21 on the first crewed flight of the Saturn V (AS-503), Apollo 8 entered lunar orbit on Christmas Eve 1968. Anders' "Earthrise" photograph during the fourth orbit became one of the most influential images in history. The crew read from Genesis on live television to ~1 billion viewers — the largest TV audience to that date. 10 orbits later they fired the SPS engine for TEI on the far side of the Moon, returning to Pacific splashdown 1968-12-27. NASA had decided in August 1968 to swap Apollo 8's payload from a high-Earth-orbit LM test to a lunar-orbit CSM-only mission after CIA intelligence suggested the USSR might attempt a circumlunar flight first.

missions/moon/artemis2.json.name: Artemis II
missions/moon/artemis2.json.first: First crewed flight beyond low-Earth orbit since Apollo 17 (1972) — and the mission that inspired this project
missions/moon/artemis2.json.description: The Artemis program's first crewed flight, and the spark that became Orrery. On 1 April 2026 NASA's SLS Block 1 launched an Orion spacecraft with four astronauts — Reid Wiseman (CDR), Victor Glover (PLT), Christina Koch (MS), and CSA's Jeremy Hansen (MS) — onto a free-return trajectory that swung them around the Moon's far side about 6,500 km above the surface and brought them home without any lunar-orbit insertion burn. At 406,771 km from Earth they travelled farther than any humans before them, beating Apollo 13's 1970 record. After a 9-day flight Orion splashed down in the Pacific off San Diego on 10 April. The flight qualified Orion's life support, navigation and heat shield for crewed missions ahead of the first landing, now planned for Artemis IV.

missions/moon/artemis4.json.name: Artemis IV
missions/moon/artemis4.json.vehicle: SLS Block 1 (last flight with the ICPS upper stage) + crewed lander (Starship HLS or Blue Moon, not yet chosen)

missions/moon/artemis4.json.first: First crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 (1972)
missions/moon/artemis4.json.description: Since NASA's February 2026 change of plan, Artemis IV is the mission that returns people to the lunar surface — the first landing since Apollo 17 in 1972, and the first ever near the south pole. SLS, on its last flight with the interim upper stage, launches Orion with four crew towards the Moon. In lunar orbit they meet a commercial lander — SpaceX's Starship or Blue Origin's Blue Moon, chosen after the Artemis III docking tests — and two astronauts descend to the south polar region for about a week of surface work, while two remain aboard Orion. The south pole is the target because its permanently shadowed craters hold water ice, which future missions may turn into drinking water, oxygen and rocket propellant. NASA has identified nine candidate landing regions. Planned for early 2028; the crew has not yet been named.

missions/moon/artemis5.json.first: Second crewed landing of the Artemis era — the start of a lunar base
missions/moon/artemis5.json.description: Artemis V is planned as the second crewed landing near the lunar south pole, following Artemis IV within the same year — part of NASA's 2026 aim of at least one landing a year. It is meant to begin the shift from short visits to a lasting presence: work towards a base on the surface, which NASA chose in March 2026 over finishing the Gateway station in lunar orbit, now paused. As on Artemis IV, SLS launches Orion with four crew and a commercial lander carries two of them down. SLS is funded to fly through Artemis V; for later missions NASA has proposed commercial, reusable alternatives. Planned for late 2028; crew, lander and landing site not yet chosen.

missions/moon/beresheet.json.payload: 585 kg launch mass; first private spacecraft to reach lunar orbit; lost during powered descent ~150 m above the surface

missions/moon/beresheet.json.first: First privately-funded mission to reach the Moon; first Israeli lunar mission
missions/moon/beresheet.json.description: SpaceIL's Beresheet (Hebrew: 'In the beginning') launched as a shared-ride passenger on a Falcon 9 in February 2019. Instead of a direct trans-lunar injection, the small lander performed weeks of perigee-raising phasing burns to climb from a parking orbit out to the Moon — a fuel-saving trajectory pioneered for low-budget missions. After successful lunar orbit insertion on 4 April 2019, an inertial measurement unit reset during descent caused the main engine to shut down. Beresheet crashed in Mare Serenitatis. SpaceIL committed to a successor (Beresheet 2) within days.

missions/moon/blue-moon-mk1.json.description: Blue Origin's first cargo Blue Moon lander, contracted under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program. A single-stage descent vehicle powered by the BE-7 cryogenic engine, designed to deliver up to ~3 tonnes of payload to the lunar surface. Launches on Blue Origin's New Glenn from Cape Canaveral, performs trans-lunar injection on the New Glenn second stage, then executes lunar orbit insertion and powered descent. The Mark 1 cargo flight precedes the human-rated Mark 2, which NASA contracted for crewed Artemis landings — now one of the two candidate landers for Artemis IV and later missions.

missions/moon/chandrayaan1.json.description: ISRO's first interplanetary spacecraft. The orbiter delivered the Moon Impact Probe to the lunar surface — the first Indian object on another world — and carried 11 instruments from 6 countries. NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3) instrument, hosted on Chandrayaan-1, made the discovery that rewrote textbooks: water molecules are widespread across the lunar surface, not just locked in polar shadowed craters. The mission ended abruptly in August 2009 when ISRO lost communication with the spacecraft.

missions/moon/chandrayaan3.json.first: First soft-landing near the lunar south pole
missions/moon/chandrayaan3.json.description: Following the loss of Chandrayaan-2's Vikram lander in 2019, ISRO's third lunar mission was deliberately conservative — focused on the lander rather than carrying an orbiter. Vikram touched down at 69.4° S latitude, the closest any spacecraft has come to a lunar pole. The Pragyan rover detected sulfur on the lunar surface for the first time and made in-situ thermal measurements. India became the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon, landing closer to a lunar pole than any spacecraft before it — a region where future water-ice mining may become possible.

missions/moon/change1.json.name: Chang'e 1
missions/moon/change1.json.payload: 2350 kg launch mass; 130 kg science payload
missions/moon/change1.json.first: China's first lunar mission and first Chinese spacecraft to reach the Moon
missions/moon/change1.json.description: The first phase of China's Lunar Exploration Program (CLEP) and CNSA's first mission beyond Earth. Launched 2007-10-24 from Xichang Satellite Launch Center on a Long March 3A, Chang'e 1 (named after the Moon goddess of Chinese folklore) entered a 200-km circular polar lunar orbit on 2007-11-07. Carried 8 instruments — a CCD stereo camera, a laser altimeter, an imaging spectrometer, gamma-ray and X-ray spectrometers, a microwave radiometer, a solar wind detector, and a high-energy particle detector. Produced China's first full lunar global topographic map at 120-200 m resolution and elemental abundance maps of Th, K, U, O, Si, Mg, Al, Ca, Ti, Fe. Mission deliberately ended 2009-03-01 with a controlled impact at 1.50° S, 52.36° E in Mare Fecunditatis — China's first object on the lunar surface, paving the way for Chang'e 3 (2013 surface landing) and Chang'e 5 (2020 sample return). Operated 16 months — 4 months past nominal.

missions/moon/change3.json.payload: 3780 kg launch mass; 1200 kg lander; 140 kg Yutu rover

missions/moon/change3.json.description: Chang'e 3 was the third lander in CNSA's Chang'e programme and the first successful soft landing on the Moon since the Soviet Luna 24 in 1976 — a 37-year gap. The Long March 3B launched on a direct lunar trajectory in December 2013, with a single mid-course correction before lunar orbit insertion. The lander touched down in Mare Imbrium on 14 December and deployed the Yutu (Jade Rabbit) rover, which operated for 31 months despite a mobility failure ending its drive on lunar day 2. Chang'e 3's lander continued imaging for years afterward.

missions/moon/change4.json.description: The lunar far side has no direct radio line of sight to Earth. To land a spacecraft there, China first launched the Queqiao relay satellite to a halo orbit around Earth-Moon Lagrange point L2 — a vantage point that sees both the far side and Earth simultaneously. With that infrastructure in place, Chang'e 4 became the first spacecraft to soft-land on the far side. The Yutu-2 rover has been operating since January 2019 and has driven ~1.6 km as of 2024, making it the longest-operating lunar rover in history.

missions/moon/change5.json.name: Chang'e 5
missions/moon/change5.json.payload: 8200 kg launch mass; 1.731 kg sample returned
missions/moon/change5.json.first: First lunar sample return in 44 years (since Luna 24, 1976)
missions/moon/change5.json.description: Chang'e 5 was the first sample return from the Moon since the Soviet Union's Luna 24 in 1976 — a 44-year gap. The architecture: orbiter + lander + ascent vehicle + sample-return capsule, all in one launch. The lander touched down at Mons Rümker, drilled and scooped 1.731 kg of regolith, lifted off, rendezvoused and docked with the orbiter (the first robotic lunar rendezvous), and the capsule returned to Earth. The samples are from a region only 2 billion years old — much younger than any Apollo or Luna sample, rewriting models of lunar volcanism.

The Queqiao-2 relay satellite was launched first (March 2024) to support the mission. Chang'e 6 then collected 1.935 kg from Apollo Crater on the far side — material with very different composition from any lunar sample previously returned. The Moon's two hemispheres are radically different (the far side has thicker crust, fewer mare); these samples may finally explain why.

missions/moon/clementine.json.first: Joint NASA-DoD lunar mission; first hints of water ice at lunar poles
missions/moon/clementine.json.description: Designed primarily as a Strategic Defense Initiative technology demonstrator, Clementine spent 10 weeks in lunar orbit returning the first systematic global topographic and multispectral map of the Moon. Bistatic radar measurements at the lunar south pole produced the first tantalising hints of water ice — confirmed years later by Lunar Prospector and Chandrayaan-1. The follow-on mission to flyby the asteroid Geographos failed when a thruster malfunction depleted the spacecraft's propellant.

missions/moon/lro.json.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
missions/moon/lro.json.description: Orbiting the Moon since 2009 at 50 km mean lunar altitude, LRO's narrow-angle camera images at 50 cm/pixel — high enough to see Apollo descent stages, rover tracks, and astronaut footpaths still preserved in the regolith. It found Lunokhod 1 thirty-nine years after the rover went dark. It identified 200+ candidate landing sites for Artemis. The water ice deposits at the lunar south pole that drive every modern lunar programme were quantified by LRO instruments. A scout mission that became the foundation of the modern lunar era.

missions/moon/luna10.json.name: Luna 10
missions/moon/luna10.json.payload: ~1582 kg launch mass; 248 kg dedicated orbiter section
missions/moon/luna10.json.first: First spacecraft to orbit the Moon (and any body other than Earth)
missions/moon/luna10.json.description: Launched 1966-03-31 from Baikonur, Luna 10 became the first spacecraft to orbit the Moon — and the first artificial satellite of any body other than Earth — when it inserted into a 350 × 1017 km lunar orbit at 71.9° inclination on 1966-04-03. Two and a half years before Apollo 8 reached the Moon with humans aboard. Carried a magnetometer, gamma-ray spectrometer, infrared radiometer, micrometeoroid detectors, plasma sensors, and a radio probe of the lunar gravity field. The gamma-ray data was the first compositional remote sensing of the Moon, suggesting basalt-like mare composition. Famously broadcast the Internationale anthem during the 23rd Congress of the Soviet Communist Party on 1966-04-04 — a propaganda flourish more than science. Operated 56 days / 460 orbits before its NiCd batteries depleted on 1966-05-30; remains in lunar orbit.

missions/moon/luna16.json.name: Luna 16
missions/moon/luna16.json.payload: 5727 kg launch mass; 1880 kg lander; 0.101 kg lunar regolith returned
missions/moon/luna16.json.first: First robotic lunar sample return; first non-American lunar samples
missions/moon/luna16.json.description: Luna 16 was the Soviet Union's first successful robotic sample-return mission and the first non-crewed lunar return of any kind. After Apollo 11 brought home 22 kg of crewed samples in 1969, Luna 16 returned 101 grams of regolith from Mare Fecunditatis a year later — a fraction of Apollo's payload, but a profound proof-of-concept for the alternative architecture. The mission used a Proton-K booster and a direct return profile: descent to the surface, drill core, ascent stage launch, ballistic return capsule to Kazakhstan. The technique was reused for Luna 20 and Luna 24, and decades later by Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6.

missions/moon/luna17.json.first: First teleoperated rover to operate on another world
missions/moon/luna17.json.description: The first wheels on the Moon — driven from a control room in Crimea. Lunokhod 1 was a 322 kg pressurised tub mounted on eight independently-driven wheels, controlled by a five-person team in real time across the 2.5-second light-speed delay. It drove 10.5 km over 11 lunar days (322 Earth days), photographed 20,000+ scenes, and operated long past its 90-day design lifetime. Lost to history in the 1970s, located again in 2010 when NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted it sitting where it stopped.

missions/moon/luna21.json.first: Second Soviet lunar rover; longest off-world drive (~39 km) for over 40 years
missions/moon/luna21.json.description: Luna 21 delivered Lunokhod 2, the Soviet Union's second crewed-controlled lunar rover, to Le Monnier crater on the southern edge of Mare Serenitatis in January 1973. The rover was driven from a control room in Crimea by a five-person team and traversed approximately 39 km over four lunar days — a record off-world distance that held until NASA's Opportunity rover passed it on Mars in 2014. Lunokhod 2 returned 80,000 television frames and 86 panoramas before dust contamination of its solar arrays ended operations.

The drilled core extracted regolith from 2 m depth and returned 170 g to Earth. A 1978 Soviet analysis reported ~0.1% water by mass in the core — an unconfirmed, still-debated result — foreshadowing later confirmed detections of lunar water. Luna 24 also marked the closure of the Soviet lunar programme; resources shifted to Mars and Venus.

missions/moon/luna9.json.payload: 1583 kg launch mass; 99 kg lander capsule
missions/moon/luna9.json.first: First soft-landing on the Moon; first photographs from the lunar surface
missions/moon/luna9.json.description: After 11 Soviet failures and 5 American Ranger missions designed only to crash, Luna 9 became the first spacecraft to soft-land on another world. Nine images — including five panoramas — returned across three sessions over three days settled a long-running scientific debate: the Moon's surface was solid, not a sea of dust deep enough to swallow a lander. The mission lasted 3 days before battery depletion. Within months, every Moon-bound mission afterwards used soft-landing as the baseline.

missions/moon/lunar-prospector.json.name: Lunar Prospector
missions/moon/lunar-prospector.json.first: Neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both lunar poles
missions/moon/lunar-prospector.json.description: The third NASA Discovery-class mission and the first NASA-managed dedicated lunar orbiter of the post-Apollo era. Launched 1998-01-07 on an Athena II from Cape Canaveral, Lunar Prospector entered a 100-km circular polar lunar orbit on 1998-01-11. The 296-kg spinning spacecraft carried five instruments: a gamma-ray spectrometer for global crustal composition, a neutron spectrometer for hydrogen / water-ice detection at the poles, an alpha-particle spectrometer for radon gas (indirect volcanism detection), a magnetometer + electron reflectometer for crustal magnetism, and a Doppler gravity experiment. Boynton-team analysis of the neutron data (Feldman et al., Science 281 + 284) found sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles — consistent with ~2 × 10⁹ tonnes of hydrogen-rich material (probably water ice) in permanently shadowed polar craters. Mission ended 1999-07-31 with deliberate impact near Shackleton crater hoping to release a detectable water-vapour plume; none was seen. The hydrogen finding stood until LCROSS and Chandrayaan-1 / M3 (2009) provided independent confirmation.

missions/moon/slim.json.payload: 730 kg launch mass; 200 kg lander; 2 micro-rovers (LEV-1, LEV-2)

missions/moon/slim.json.description: Until SLIM, lunar landings had a kilometre-scale targeting accuracy. JAXA's Smart Lander demonstrated 100 m accuracy — the precision required for crewed missions to dock with pre-positioned cargo, for sample-return ascent vehicles to find their orbital partners, and for any future architecture that depends on landing at specific scientifically valuable sites. SLIM also pioneered low-energy ballistic transfer to the Moon, taking 135 days to arrive but using less propellant than direct trajectories. A demonstration of the patience interplanetary missions can afford when timeline isn't the binding constraint.

missions/moon/smart-1.json.name: SMART-1
missions/moon/smart-1.json.payload: 367 kg launch mass; 1.2 kW solar-electric Hall-effect ion thruster
missions/moon/smart-1.json.first: First European spacecraft to reach the Moon; first mission to reach the Moon under ion propulsion
missions/moon/smart-1.json.description: ESA's first lunar mission and the first European spacecraft to reach the Moon. SMART = Small Missions for Advanced Research in Technology — and the key technology was a Hall-effect solar-electric ion thruster (PPS-1350-G), at the time the largest such thruster ever flown. Launched 2003-09-27 as a shared payload on an Ariane 5 from Kourou, the 367-kg spacecraft used its 1.2-kW xenon ion drive over 13 months to slowly raise its Earth orbit, eventually captured by lunar gravity on 2004-11-15 — a 13-month low-thrust spiral rather than the days-long chemical transfer of every prior lunar mission. Operated for 16 months in a polar lunar orbit returning AMIE camera imagery, the first X-ray fluorescence elemental maps of the Moon (D-CIXS), and infrared mineral spectroscopy (SIR). Deliberately impacted Lacus Excellentiae (34.4° S, 46.2° W) on 2006-09-03 05:42 UTC — the impact flash was observed live from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope.
