missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.name: Voyager 2
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.payload: Planetary flyby spacecraft; RTG electrical power
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.first: Only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune; Grand Tour of four giant planets
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.dispatch: Voyager 2 flew the tour that may never be flown again. Launched sixteen days before its twin on a slower, longer arc, it is the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune — two worlds that remain, decades later, known to us almost entirely from the few hours it spent racing past each one. It found a planet tipped on its side, the fastest winds in the solar system, and a frozen moon venting geysers into space, and then it too crossed into interstellar space, in 2018. Every serious plan to return to the ice giants still rests on what this single spacecraft saw on its way out.
missions/neptune/voyager-2.json.description: The twin that kept going when budgets tightened, Voyager 2 carried the Grand Tour from Jupiter and Saturn out to Uranus and Neptune — still the only close-up images we have of the ice giants. Its Neptune encounter in 1989 revealed the Great Dark Spot and Triton's geysers. Today both Voyagers sail in interstellar space with a golden record as humanity's calling card. Orrery lists Neptune as the catalogue destination; the real path relied on multiple gravity assists.

missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.name: New Horizons
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.payload: New Horizons flyby spacecraft; RTG power
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.first: First flyby of Pluto and its moons; sharpest images of a Kuiper belt world
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.dispatch: New Horizons had exactly one chance and took it. There was no orbit and no way to slow down — nine and a half years of travel, the fastest launch in history, all converging on a few hours at Pluto, executed by a machine so far away that each command took hours to arrive. It nailed the flyby on 14 July 2015 and overturned the expectation of a dead world: Pluto turned out to have mountains of water ice, a vast heart-shaped glacier of frozen nitrogen still slowly churning, and a young, active surface no one thought a body that small and cold could keep. Then it flew on to Arrokoth, a billion kilometres past Pluto — the most distant world ever seen up close — and it is still going.
missions/pluto/new-horizons.json.description: A nine-year sprint after the fastest launch to date, New Horizons compressed decades of anticipation into one July 2015 day — a world turned from a pixelated blur into mountains of water ice and nitrogen glaciers on Pluto's heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio. The spacecraft later flew Arrokoth, linking the mission to the primordial solar system. Flight arcs in Orrery are direct-transfer teaching models, not the actual Jupiter gravity assist.

missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.name: Psyche
missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.payload: 2747 kg launch mass (1648 kg dry; 1085 kg xenon propellant)
missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.first: First mission to a metal-rich M-class asteroid; first use of Hall-effect ion thrusters as the primary cruise propulsion
missions/psyche/psyche-mission.json.description: Psyche reaches for the exposed nickel-iron core of a differentiated proto-planet — a 226-km metal body that may be the closest analogue to Earth's own core anywhere accessible. Launched 2023-10-13 on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy LC-39A. Four SPT-140 Hall-effect ion thrusters spiral the trajectory outward; a Mars gravity assist in May 2026 (4,609 km closest approach) added the energy ion thrust alone couldn't deliver in time. Arrival planned 2029-08, followed by a 26-month four-orbit-phase descent (A → B → C → D) mapping the asteroid's gravity, magnetism, topography, and composition. If the metal-core hypothesis is right, Psyche will look unlike anything else we've visited — bare metal surface, iron-sulphide deposits, none of the rubble-pile chaos of typical asteroids.

missions/saturn/cassini.json.name: Cassini-Huygens
missions/saturn/cassini.json.payload: Saturn orbiter (~5712 kg dry) + Huygens descent probe (~318 kg, ESA-built, landed on Titan 2005-01-14)
missions/saturn/cassini.json.first: 13 years in orbit around Saturn — Huygens landed on Titan 2005-01-14 (first outer-solar-system soft landing)
missions/saturn/cassini.json.dispatch: Cassini did what no spacecraft had done at any giant planet: it stopped. For thirteen years it lived at Saturn, and the discoveries that mattered most came from staying — the geysers of Enceladus, caught because the orbiter flew close enough, often enough, to see a tiny moon venting its hidden ocean into space. It dropped Europe’s Huygens probe onto Titan, the only landing ever made in the outer solar system, and charted a world of methane rivers and lakes. At the end, out of fuel, it was flown deliberately into Saturn so it could never fall onto the ocean moons it had found and contaminate them — a mission that closed by protecting the places it discovered.
missions/saturn/cassini.json.description: Joint NASA-ESA-ASI mission. After a 7-year cruise using gravity assists at Venus, Earth, and Jupiter, Cassini entered Saturn orbit 2004-07-01 and operated for 13 years, completing 294 orbits and 162 close moon flybys. It discovered Enceladus’s south-polar plumes (active water-ice geysers), mapped Titan’s methane lakes via radar, and resolved Saturn’s hexagonal polar storm. The Grand Finale (April–September 2017) wove 22 orbits through the gap between the rings and the cloud tops, ending with a controlled atmospheric entry to prevent any chance of contaminating Enceladus or Titan with terrestrial microbes.

events.label: VENUS GRAVITY ASSIST
events.note: First of four assists building the energy for Saturn arrival.

events.label: SATURN ORBIT INSERTION
events.note: Main engine burn places Cassini into Saturn orbit, beginning the 13-year tour.

missions/saturn/huygens.json.name: Huygens
missions/saturn/huygens.json.payload: 318 kg ESA entry probe — aeroshell, 3 parachutes, 6 science packages (HASI, GCMS, DISR, ACP, SSP, DWE). Designed to survive 2.5-hour atmospheric descent through Titan's nitrogen–methane atmosphere to the surface.
missions/saturn/huygens.json.delta_v: ~6 km/s (entry deceleration from 6 km/s hypersonic to surface)
missions/saturn/huygens.json.first: First and only soft landing in the outer solar system — parachuted through Titan's atmosphere on 2005-01-14
missions/saturn/huygens.json.dispatch: Huygens was sent not to orbit but to fall. Strapped to Cassini for seven years, it detached on Christmas Day 2004 and coasted alone toward Titan for twenty days. When it hit Titan's atmosphere at six kilometres per second, a heat shield bought the time it needed; then three parachute stages slowed it for two and a half hours through an orange haze no instrument had ever crossed. It photographed river valleys, measured wind speeds, smelled the atmosphere — and touched down on a floodplain of rounded water-ice pebbles. It was the first landing ever made in the outer solar system, and no spacecraft has landed there since.
missions/saturn/huygens.json.description: ESA's Huygens probe rode aboard NASA's Cassini spacecraft on a 7-year interplanetary cruise to the Saturn system, arriving at Saturn in July 2004. Released on 2004-12-25, it coasted for 20 days before entering Titan's nitrogen–methane atmosphere on 2005-01-14 at 6 km/s. An aeroshell slowed the probe to subsonic speed; three successive parachute stages then guided it through 2 hours 27 minutes of descent, collecting the first direct measurements of Titan's atmosphere — temperature, pressure, wind, and chemical composition at all altitudes. The probe transmitted 350 images during descent and continued transmitting from the surface for 72 minutes, revealing a floodplain of rounded water-ice pebbles beneath a thin veneer of liquid methane at 10.3°S, 192.3°W.

missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.name: Pioneer 11
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.payload: Outer-system flyby spacecraft; SNAP-19 RTGs (~165 W at launch); twin of Pioneer 10
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.first: First spacecraft to fly past Saturn (1979-09-01); demonstrated the gravity-assist that sent Voyager 2 onward
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.dispatch: Pioneer 11 was the second scout, and it went further than its twin. After its own pass by Jupiter it used the planet’s gravity to cross the solar system and reach Saturn in 1979 — the first spacecraft ever to do so — deliberately flying through the ring plane to test whether the region was safe. It found the gap the Voyagers would thread a year later. Much of what made the Grand Tour possible was this: a small, cheap probe sent ahead to take the risks and map the hazards, so the flagships behind it could fly with confidence instead of fear.
missions/saturn/pioneer-11.json.description: Twin of Pioneer 10, launched a year later. Pioneer 11 used Jupiter’s gravity to bend its trajectory toward Saturn — the canonical proof of gravity-assist propulsion, the technique that later enabled the Voyager Grand Tour. At Saturn it discovered the F ring and a small inner moon later resolved into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus. Carries the same Pioneer plaque as its twin. Signal lost 1995-09-30 from a heliocentric distance of ~43 AU; the spacecraft is now heading toward the constellation Aquila.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas-Centaur from Cape Canaveral on a Jupiter-Saturn gravity-assist trajectory.

events.label: JUPITER FLYBY
events.note: Used Jupiter assist to bend onto a Saturn-bound path.

events.label: SATURN CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: First images of the planet at close range; discovered the F ring and a small inner moon (later resolved into the co-orbital pair Janus/Epimetheus).

missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.name: Voyager 1
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.payload: Planetary flyby spacecraft; three RTG modules totalling ~470 W at launch (decaying to ~250 W today)
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.first: Most distant human-made object — currently ~170 AU from the Sun in interstellar space
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.dispatch: Voyager 1 is the farthest thing humanity has ever made, and it got there almost by an accident of geometry. A close pass by Saturn’s giant moon Titan — chosen for the science — bent its path up and out of the plane of the planets and aimed it at the edge of the solar system, and it has been climbing ever since. Along the way it found active volcanoes on Io, the first ever seen off Earth, and in 1990 it turned back to take the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it became the first machine to cross into interstellar space. It is still transmitting, on fading nuclear power, from more than a hundred times the Earth’s distance from the Sun.
missions/saturn/voyager-1.json.description: Launched 16 days after Voyager 2, Voyager 1 flew faster and arrived at Jupiter first (1979) and Saturn first (1980). Its Titan flyby bent the trajectory upward out of the ecliptic plane, ending the planetary tour but sending it on the most direct path to the heliopause — which it crossed on 2012-08-25, the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. From a heliocentric distance of ~6 billion km it took the Pale Blue Dot family portrait (1990-02-14), the photograph Carl Sagan wrote about. Both Voyagers carry the Golden Record as humanity’s calling card.

events.label: JUPITER CLOSEST APPROACH
events.note: Flyby at ~349,000 km; discovered Io volcanism, mapped Europa’s surface.

events.label: SATURN + TITAN FLYBYS

missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.name: Parker Solar Probe
missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.vehicle: Delta IV Heavy + Star 48BV third stage
missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.payload: 685 kg (including 11.43-cm carbon-carbon Thermal Protection System sustaining 1,377 °C at perihelion)
missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.first: Closest spacecraft to the Sun ever flown (6.1 M km, 9.86 R☉); first spacecraft to enter the solar corona (2021-04-28); fastest human-made object (~191 km/s)
missions/sun/parker-solar-probe.json.description: Parker Solar Probe ran the highest-energy launch ever flown for a science mission — C3 of 154 km²/s², requiring a custom Star 48BV solid third stage atop a Delta IV Heavy just to escape Earth into a Sun-falling trajectory. Seven Venus gravity assists over six years progressively lowered perihelion from 0.16 AU (P1, 2018-11-05) to 0.046 AU (P22, 2024-12-24 — 9.86 solar radii, 6.1 million km from the surface). At P8 in 2021-04-28 Parker dipped below the Alfvén critical surface — the first spacecraft ever to enter the Sun's corona. At P22 it reached ~191 km/s, becoming the fastest human-made object ever. The 11.43-cm carbon-carbon heat shield sustained 1,377 °C while the spacecraft bus 1 metre behind it remained at room temperature.

missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.name: Solar Orbiter
missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.payload: 1800 kg (incl. 209 kg of instruments + heat shield)
missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.first: First mission designed to image the Sun's polar regions in detail; complements Parker Solar Probe's in-corona measurements with high-latitude remote sensing
missions/sun/solar-orbiter.json.description: ESA-led mission with a NASA launch and one instrument contribution. Where Parker Solar Probe goes closer than anyone has ever been, Solar Orbiter goes higher — using repeated Venus gravity assists over a decade to climb out of the ecliptic toward ~33° heliographic inclination. From that vantage point its instrument suite (PHI, EUI, SPICE, STIX, METIS, SoloHI + four in-situ packages) images the Sun's polar magnetic fields, traces solar-wind acceleration in real time, and links remote and in-situ measurements simultaneously. First perihelion 2020-06-15 at 0.51 AU. Closest perihelion to date 2022-10-12 at 0.29 AU (inside Mercury's perihelion).

missions/sun/ulysses.json.name: Ulysses
missions/sun/ulysses.json.payload: 366 kg spin-stabilised, 9 instruments (magnetometer, solar wind, energetic particles, radio + plasma waves, dust, cosmic rays, gamma-ray burst detector, solar-wind composition, X-ray + gamma-ray bursts). Powered by a single GPHS-RTG.
missions/sun/ulysses.json.delta_v: ~15.4 km/s (Jupiter gravity assist did the heavy lifting)
missions/sun/ulysses.json.first: Only spacecraft ever to enter a high-inclination heliocentric orbit; only direct measurements of the solar wind at all heliographic latitudes
missions/sun/ulysses.json.description: Joint ESA / NASA mission. Launched 1990-10-06 from STS-41 Discovery + IUS + PAM-S upper stages, Ulysses used a Jupiter gravity assist on 1992-02-08 to deflect itself ~80° out of the ecliptic — the only way to reach a near-polar Sun-relative orbit from Earth's near-equatorial orbital plane. Three full polar orbits of the Sun over 18.5 years mapped the solar wind, heliospheric magnetic field, and energetic particles at all heliographic latitudes — direct measurements that revealed how solar-wind structure varies between equatorial slow-wind regions and high-latitude fast-wind streams from coronal holes. Mission terminated 2009-06-30 when thruster hydrazine froze in the lines. Hardware remains in heliocentric polar orbit.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: STS-41 Discovery deploys Ulysses + IUS / PAM-S upper stages.

events.label: JUPITER FLYBY
events.note: Gravity assist deflects Ulysses ~80° out of the ecliptic into a polar Sun-relative orbit.

events.label: FIRST SOUTH POLAR PASS
events.note: First-ever direct measurements of solar wind over a Sun pole.

events.label: FIRST NORTH POLAR PASS
events.note: Completion of the first full solar polar orbit.

events.label: MISSION END
events.note: Thruster lines freeze; final command issued 2009-06-30.

missions/venus/akatsuki.json.name: Akatsuki
missions/venus/akatsuki.json.first: Recovered from a 5-year solar-orbit hold to achieve Venus orbit on a backup attempt; the only Venus orbiter active in its final years of operation
missions/venus/akatsuki.json.description: Akatsuki — "dawn" — was Japan's first Venus mission. Launched 2010-05-20 from Tanegashima on an H-IIA 202, paired with the IKAROS solar-sail demonstrator. The planned Venus orbit insertion 2010-12-07 failed when salt crystal buildup in an oxidiser check valve threw the main engine off-axis 152 seconds into the burn. JAXA kept the spacecraft alive in solar orbit for five years, twelve correction maneuvers, until the next Venus encounter window. On 2015-12-07 a 1228-second burn using four attitude-control thrusters — never designed for orbital insertion — placed Akatsuki into a highly elliptical 400 × 440,000 km, 3°-inclination orbit. One of the most dramatic mission-saves in spaceflight history. Contact was lost in 2024; JAXA declared operations complete on 2025-09-18.

missions/venus/magellan.json.name: Magellan
missions/venus/magellan.json.vehicle: Space Shuttle Atlantis (STS-30) + Inertial Upper Stage
missions/venus/magellan.json.first: Most complete radar map of Venus — 98% of the surface at ~120-m resolution; first planetary spacecraft launched from the Space Shuttle
missions/venus/magellan.json.description: Magellan turned Venus from a featureless cloud-veiled disc into a mapped planet. Launched from Shuttle Atlantis's payload bay 1989-05-04 — the first planetary spacecraft to ride a Shuttle — and arrived at Venus 1990-08-10 via a long Type-IV trajectory (1.5 solar revolutions). Over four mapping cycles the synthetic-aperture radar imaged 98% of Venus's surface at ~120-m resolution, revealing tessera highlands, coronae, pancake domes, and a young, volcanically-resurfaced surface. Mission ended 1994-10-13 in the Termination Experiment — the first planned controlled atmospheric entry of a planetary spacecraft.

events.note: STS-30 / Atlantis from Kennedy LC-39B; IUS deployed from Shuttle bay.

events.note: Solid-motor burn into a 295 × 8543 km, 85.5° near-polar orbit.

events.label: MAPPING CYCLE 1 COMPLETE
events.note: First full pass — 84% surface coverage at 100 m resolution.

events.label: TERMINATION EXPERIMENT
events.note: 1994-10-13. Periapsis lowered into atmosphere — first planned planetary spacecraft entry.

missions/venus/vega-1.json.name: Vega 1
missions/venus/vega-1.json.payload: 4920 kg flyby bus + ~1500 kg descent module (Venera-type lander + first-of-kind helium balloon aerostat). Twin spacecraft Vega 1 / Vega 2 launched 6 days apart for the same Venus-then-Halley itinerary.
missions/venus/vega-1.json.first: First-ever balloon aerostat deployed in another planet's atmosphere (Venus, 1985); first spacecraft to carry science to two distinct solar-system targets
missions/venus/vega-1.json.description: Soviet–ESA flagship of the Halley armada. Vega 1 launched 1984-12-15 with a Venera-lineage lander plus a first-of-kind ESA/CNES-built helium balloon that drifted in Venus's cloud deck at 54 km altitude for 46.5 hours, transmitting wind + temperature data via a 20-station global radio net. After dropping its descent module the bus used Venus gravity assist to redirect to comet 1P/Halley, achieving a 8890 km closest approach on 1986-03-06 — the first cometary nucleus encounter, and the position fix that ESA's Giotto used to navigate its own much closer Halley flyby a week later.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K / D-1 lifts Vega 1 from Baikonur.

events.label: VENUS ENCOUNTER
events.note: Descent module separates + lands; balloon deploys at 54 km altitude for 46.5 hours.

events.label: HALLEY FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach to comet 1P/Halley at 8890 km — first cometary nucleus observation.

missions/venus/vega-2.json.name: Vega 2
missions/venus/vega-2.json.payload: Identical twin of Vega 1: 4920 kg flyby bus + ~1500 kg Venus lander + helium aerostat. Launched 6 days after Vega 1 for redundancy + a paired Halley armada solution.
missions/venus/vega-2.json.first: First chemical analysis of Venusian highland-type soil (Aphrodite Terra, 1985); paired Halley encounter with Vega 1 fed Giotto's targeting solution
missions/venus/vega-2.json.description: Twin of Vega 1, launched 6 days later (1984-12-21) for redundancy + a paired Halley armada solution. Vega 2's descent module landed 1985-06-15 in Rusalka Planitia, on the northern flank of Aphrodite Terra, and used XRF spectrometry to find anorthosite-norite-troctolite material — the first chemical analysis of highland-type Venusian crust (the composition resembles lunar highlands, though the landing site itself is a plain). Its balloon performed identically to Vega 1's, drifting in the opposite hemisphere at ~240 km/h. The bus flew past comet 1P/Halley at 8030 km on 1986-03-09. Together the two Vega buses returned the first close-up cometary-nucleus images and refined the position fix that allowed Giotto to attempt a 596 km flyby five days later.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K / D-1 lifts Vega 2 from Baikonur 6 days behind Vega 1.

events.label: VENUS ENCOUNTER
events.note: Descent module lands at Aphrodite Terra (Rusalka Planitia) + returns first chemical analysis of highland-type Venusian crust.

events.label: HALLEY FLYBY
events.note: Closest approach to comet 1P/Halley at 8030 km — paired position fix for Giotto.

missions/venus/venera-13.json.name: Venera 13
missions/venus/venera-13.json.payload: ~4500 kg combined: flyby bus + 1645 kg titanium descent capsule (cameras, X-ray fluorescence soil-composition spectrometer, seismometer, soil-sampling arm with hermetic-vault drill). Designed for one of the most hostile descent environments ever attempted.
missions/venus/venera-13.json.first: Longest surface survival of any Venus mission (127 min); first colour panoramic images and first audio from another planet's surface
missions/venus/venera-13.json.description: The peak of the Soviet Venera program. Venera 13 launched 1981-10-30 and landed 1982-03-01 at 7.5°S 303°E in the Phoebe Regio highlands. Surface conditions at touchdown: 457 °C, 89 bar, sulfuric-acid haze. The lander survived 127 minutes — nearly an hour beyond its design target — returning the first colour panoramas from another planet's surface, recording wind microphone audio, and using its drill + onboard X-ray fluorescence spectrometer to determine that the basalt at the landing site was a weakly differentiated leucite alkaline composition. Twin spacecraft Venera 14 performed identical operations at a separate site five days later. The Venera series (1967–1983) remains the only successful surface program at Venus to date.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Proton-K / D-1 lifts Venera 13 from Baikonur on a 122-day cruise.

events.label: VENUS SURFACE LANDING
events.note: Touchdown in Phoebe Regio at 7.5°S 303°E; 127 minutes of surface operations under 457 °C / 89 bar.
